skills.objective: Students decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, find the constant of proportionality from a table, graph, equation or description, and use y = kx to solve problems.
skills.studentObjective: I can tell when two quantities are proportional, find the constant of proportionality, and use it to find missing values.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how I know a relationship is proportional using because, but and so with the words constant of proportionality, unit rate and origin.
successCriteria: I divide y by x in several pairs and check that the result never changes.
I name the constant of proportionality and say what it means in the situation.
I write an equation of the form y = kx and use it to find a missing value.
I explain why a straight line that misses the origin is not proportional.
skills.bigIdea: In a proportional relationship the ratio of the two quantities never changes, so one quantity is always the same multiple of the other.

syntax: The relationship is proportional because ___ divided by ___ is always ___.
The constant of proportionality is ___, which means ___ for every 1 ___.
discourse: Test several pairs of values before drawing a conclusion
Contrast a proportional case with one that only looks proportional

domains.listening: Students listen to two market price descriptions and decide which one stays the same per pound.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they tested the pairs and what the constant means in the situation.
domains.reading: Students read a short report about two toy rovers and mark each pair of distance and time.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that justifies why a relationship is or is not proportional.

vocab.def: Two quantities whose ratio is the same in every pair of values.
vocab.example: Distance and time for a rover that moves 1.5 meters every second
vocab.nonExample: Cost with a 5 dollar fee plus 2 dollars for each item
vocab.sentence: The rover's distance and time show a proportional relationship.
vocab.morphology: pro- means for, and portion means share, so the shares stay in step

vocab.def: The fixed number k in y = kx; it equals y divided by x in every pair.
vocab.example: k = 1.5 in the equation d = 1.5t
vocab.nonExample: The 3 in y = x + 3, which is added, not multiplied
vocab.sentence: The constant of proportionality for the first rover is 1.5.

vocab.def: A rate that tells how much of one quantity goes with exactly 1 of the other.
vocab.example: 1.5 meters per second
vocab.nonExample: 12 meters in 8 seconds, which is not yet compared to 1 second
vocab.sentence: The unit rate tells how far the rover moves in 1 second.

vocab.def: The point (0, 0) where the x-axis and the y-axis cross.
vocab.example: The graph of the first rover passes through the origin
vocab.nonExample: The point (0, 6) on the y-axis
vocab.sentence: A proportional graph is a straight line through the origin.
vocab.everyday: The place where something comes from or begins

vocab.def: A number that does not change; it stays the same in every pair.
vocab.example: The 1.5 you get in every row of the rover table
vocab.nonExample: The distance, which grows every second
vocab.sentence: In a proportional table the ratio stays constant.
vocab.everyday: Happening all the time without stopping

misconceptions.belief: Any graph that is a straight line shows a proportional relationship.
misconceptions.why: Students remember that proportional graphs are lines and forget that the line must also pass through the origin.
misconceptions.fix: Plot the point for 0 seconds. Ask what a proportional relationship must give when the first quantity is 0, then compare two lines.

errorCase.story: A second rover starts 6 meters ahead of the line and moves 2 meters each second.
steps: After 3 seconds it is at 12 meters, and after 6 seconds it is at 18 meters.
The two points lie on a straight line.
So the distance is proportional to the time.
errorCase.explain: A straight line is not enough. Divide each distance by its time: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3. The ratios differ, and the line crosses the y-axis at 6, not at the origin.

misconceptions.belief: The constant of proportionality is the amount that y goes up each time x goes up.
misconceptions.why: In many tables students look down a column for the pattern and describe the change instead of the ratio.
misconceptions.fix: Add a column for y ÷ x and check the result in each row. Use the constant in y = kx and test it on one row.

errorCase.story: A lemonade stand table shows 2 cups for 3 dollars, 4 cups for 6 dollars and 6 cups for 9 dollars.
steps: The cups go 2, 4, 6 and the dollars go 3, 6, 9.
The dollars go up by 3 each time, so the constant of proportionality is 3.
So the equation is y = 3x.
errorCase.explain: The constant is the ratio y ÷ x, not the jump. 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5, so y = 1.5x. Check: 1.5 × 4 = 6.

misconceptions.belief: A unit rate can be found by dividing the quantities in either order.
misconceptions.why: Students divide the smaller number by the larger number without asking which quantity the rate is measured per.
misconceptions.fix: Say the rate in words first: meters per second means meters go on top. Write the units next to each number.

errorCase.story: A rover moves 12 meters in 8 seconds.
steps: The rover moves 12 meters in 8 seconds.
To find the unit rate I divide 8 ÷ 12, which is about 0.67 meters per second.
errorCase.explain: Meters per second means meters ÷ seconds: 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 meters per second. Dividing 8 ÷ 12 gives seconds per meter.

misconceptions.belief: A rate can only describe speed.
misconceptions.why: Speed is the most common rate students meet, so the word rate seems to belong to motion only.
misconceptions.fix: Collect rates from price, work and growth: dollars per pound, pages per hour, centimeters per day. Say each one with the word per.

reading.title: Two Rovers on the Track
reading.text: The robotics club at Westfield Middle School tests a toy rover on a flat track. After 8 seconds the rover has gone 12 meters, after 12 seconds it has gone 18 meters, and after 20 seconds it has gone 30 meters. Priya divides each distance by its time and gets 1.5 every time. That number is the constant of proportionality, and it is also the unit rate: 1.5 meters per second. Because the ratio never changes, distance and time form a proportional relationship. Its graph is a straight line through the origin. A second rover starts 6 meters ahead of the line and moves 2 meters each second. After 3 seconds it is at 12 meters, and after 6 seconds it is at 18 meters. The ratios 4 and 3 are different, so the second rover is not proportional.
reading.simple: The robotics club tests a toy rover. After 8 seconds it has gone 12 meters. After 12 seconds it has gone 18 meters. After 20 seconds it has gone 30 meters. Priya divides each distance by its time and gets 1.5 every time. This is the constant of proportionality and the unit rate. A second rover starts 6 meters ahead and moves 2 meters each second. After 3 seconds it is at 12 meters. After 6 seconds it is at 18 meters. The ratios 4 and 3 are different. The second rover is not proportional.

questions.q: How far has the first rover gone after 20 seconds?
questions.a: 30 meters

questions.q: Why is the second rover not proportional even though it moves at a steady speed?
questions.a: It starts 6 meters ahead, so distance divided by time changes (4, then 3) and its graph misses the origin.

questions.q: Write an equation that links the distance d and the time t for the first rover.

wdntb.why: y = x + 4 is not proportional because it adds 4 instead of multiplying by a constant. The other three have the form y = kx.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at the table: 2 seconds and 3 meters, 4 seconds and 6 meters, 8 seconds and 12 meters. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If a relationship is proportional, the point (0, 0) is on its graph.
asn.why: When the first quantity is 0, the second must be 0 too, because y = kx and k times 0 is 0.

asn.claim: If a graph is a straight line, the relationship is proportional.
asn.why: It is proportional only when the line also passes through the origin.

wyr.q: Would you rather check a proportional relationship by dividing in a table or by looking at a graph?
wyr.a: Divide y by x in a table
wyr.b: Look for a line through the origin

compare.a: Ines divides distance by time in three rows and gets 4 each time.
compare.b: Jon sees the distance go up by 4 each row, so he says it is proportional.
compare.prompt: Whose test proves the relationship is proportional? What would Jon need to check?

debate.claim: A plan that charges a fee plus a price for each item is proportional.
debate.forEvidence: The graph is a straight line, and the cost goes up by the same amount for each item.
debate.againstEvidence: With a 5 dollar fee, 0 items still cost 5 dollars, so the graph misses the origin and the ratio changes.

listening.script: Listen to Omar at the farmers market. I sell almonds by weight. Two pounds cost 14 dollars, and five pounds cost 35 dollars. Fourteen divided by two is seven, and thirty-five divided by five is also seven. So almonds cost 7 dollars for every pound. My neighbor Elena sells pecans. Two pounds cost 15 dollars, and four pounds cost 27 dollars, because she adds a 3 dollar bag fee once. Fifteen divided by two is seven and a half, but twenty-seven divided by four is six and three quarters. The ratio changes, so her prices are not proportional.

tasks.q: What is the unit rate for the almonds?
tasks.why: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 and 35 ÷ 5 = 7, so almonds cost 7 dollars for every pound.

tasks.q: Why are Elena's pecan prices not proportional?
options: The 3 dollar bag fee is added once, so the cost per pound changes.
tasks.why: The cost per pound is 7.50 for 2 pounds and 6.75 for 4 pounds, so there is no constant ratio.

story.title: The Market Price Board
story.goal: write a price board that stays fair for every size of bag
story.intro: Zoe helps her uncle sell dried fruit. Customers ask for different amounts, and she wants one clear rule that gives a fair price every time.

beats.lead: Zoe studies the first three bags her uncle priced and looks for what stays the same.
beats.success: Zoe finds the same price for every pound, and she writes the constant at the top of the board.
beats.redirect: The prices do not seem to match one rule, so Zoe looks again at what changes and what stays the same.

beats.lead: A customer asks for a bag size that is not on the board.
beats.success: Zoe uses her equation to find the price at once, and the customer nods.
beats.redirect: The price feels too high, so Zoe checks her equation against a bag she already knows.

beats.lead: Her uncle suggests adding a flat bag fee to the board.
beats.success: Zoe sees that a fee would break the constant, and she explains the change to her uncle.
beats.redirect: Zoe wonders if the fee changes the pattern, so she tests two bag sizes and compares the ratios.

story.ending: The price board is clear and fair, and Zoe can say exactly why the prices are proportional.

panels.says: The bike stand charges 5 dollars for 2 hours and 10 dollars for 4 hours.
Then one hour costs 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 dollars. Does that work for 4 hours?
Yes, because 10 ÷ 4 is also 2.5. The ratio stays constant.
So the graph passes through the origin: 0 hours cost 0 dollars.

predict.q: A third customer rents a bike for 6 hours at the same rate. Predict the cost.
predict.why: The constant is 2.5 dollars per hour, so 6 hours cost 6 × 2.5 = 15 dollars.

transfer.relationship: The second quantity is always the same multiple of the first, so y ÷ x never changes
phrasings: The rover travels 1.5 meters for each second
A table in which d ÷ t is 1.5 in every row
A straight-line graph through (0, 0) and (4, 6)

decoys.why: This adds 1.5 instead of multiplying, so the ratio changes from row to row.
The slope is 1.5, but the line misses the origin, so it is not proportional.

modeling.title: Planning the rover track time
modeling.scenario: A fictional robotics club has a rover that moves at a constant speed along a straight track. The club wants to know if the battery lasts for the whole run.
assumptions: The rover moves at exactly the same speed the whole time.
The rover starts at the beginning of the track.
The battery gives full power until it is empty.
prompts: Write an equation for the distance d after t seconds. How long does the rover need for 45 meters?
Is 40 seconds of battery enough for the track? Explain with your equation.
The club builds a 66 meter track. Can the same battery finish it?
limits: A real rover speeds up and slows down, so the constant speed is only an approximation.
A heavier load or a rough floor would change the rate.

sentence.base: The rover's distance and time are proportional.
sentence.because: The rover's distance and time are proportional because the distance divided by the time is always 1.5.
sentence.but: The second rover moves at a steady speed, but its distance and time are not proportional.
sentence.so: The distance divided by the time is always 1.5, so the graph passes through the origin.

diagnostic.prompt: A table shows 3 pounds for 12 dollars, 5 pounds for 20 dollars and 8 pounds for 32 dollars. Is the relationship proportional? Show how you know and write an equation.
lookFor: Divides cost by pounds in more than one row and gets 4 each time
Names 4 dollars per pound as the constant
Writes y = 4x with the variables defined
diagnostic.language: Let the student point to the row and say the division before writing a sentence. If the divisions are correct, the barrier is language, not the idea of a constant ratio.

extension.task: Make a table of four pairs that is proportional and a second table of four pairs that is not, with the same first pair. Graph both.
extension.reasoning: Write a convincing argument that your second table is not proportional, using at least two ratios.

en.learning: Your child is learning that two amounts are proportional when one is always the same number of times the other, like 7 dollars for every pound of almonds.
en.say: Divide the price by the amount. If you get the same number every time, the prices are proportional.
en.ask: If 3 pounds of rice cost 12 dollars, how much do 5 pounds cost, and how do you know?
en.activity: At the store, pick two items sold by weight. Ask your child to find the price for 1 pound of each and write a rule for the total cost.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo que dos cantidades son proporcionales cuando una siempre es el mismo número de veces la otra, como 7 dólares por cada libra de almendras.
es.say: Dividan el precio entre la cantidad. Si obtienen el mismo número cada vez, los precios son proporcionales.
es.ask: Si 3 libras de arroz cuestan 12 dólares, ¿cuánto cuestan 5 libras y cómo lo saben?
es.activity: En la tienda, escojan dos productos que se venden por peso. Pidan a su hijo o hija que calcule el precio de 1 libra de cada uno y que escriba una regla para el costo total.

skills.objective: Students solve multi-step percent problems such as discounts, markups, tax, interest and percent increase or decrease, and explain which amount the percent is taken from.
skills.studentObjective: I can solve percent problems about prices and changes, and I can say which amount the percent is taken from.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain a percent calculation using because, but and so with the words original amount, discount and percent change.
successCriteria: I name the original amount before I calculate with a percent.
I find a discount, markup or tax as a percent of the correct amount.
I find a percent change by dividing the change by the original amount.
I explain in a full sentence why two equal percents can give different amounts.
skills.bigIdea: A percent is always a percent of some starting amount, so changing the starting amount changes what the same percent means.

syntax: The discount is ___% of the original amount, which is ___.
The price changed from ___ to ___, so the percent change is ___.
discourse: Describe each step of a price calculation in order
Explain why a second percent is taken from a different amount

domains.listening: Students listen to a fundraiser plan and follow the markup and then the tax.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner which amount each percent is taken from and why.
domains.reading: Students read a short shop story and underline each price and the percent attached to it.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that explains a sale price.

vocab.def: How much an amount went up or down, written as a percent of the original amount.
vocab.example: A price rises from 40 dollars to 46 dollars: an increase of 15%
vocab.nonExample: The change in dollars alone, 6 dollars, with no comparison to the original
vocab.sentence: The percent change from 40 dollars to 46 dollars is an increase of 15%.

vocab.def: An amount taken off a price, often given as a percent of the original price.
vocab.example: 25% off a 60 dollar pair of cleats is a 15 dollar discount
vocab.nonExample: The sale price of 45 dollars, which is what remains after the discount
vocab.sentence: The shop gives a discount on the cleats.

vocab.def: An amount a seller adds to the cost to set the selling price.
vocab.example: A ball costs the shop 8 dollars and gets a 4 dollar markup
vocab.nonExample: A discount, which lowers the price instead of raising it
vocab.sentence: The markup on the ball is 50% of its cost.

vocab.def: Money earned or paid for using money over time, found as a percent of the amount.
vocab.example: 4% simple interest on 300 dollars is 12 dollars in one year
vocab.nonExample: Wanting to learn about a hobby
vocab.sentence: The savings account pays interest each year.
vocab.everyday: A feeling of wanting to learn or know more about something

vocab.def: The starting amount that a percent is taken from.
vocab.example: The 60 dollar price before the discount
vocab.nonExample: The 45 dollar sale price after the discount
vocab.sentence: Every percent in a price problem is taken from an original amount.

misconceptions.belief: If a price goes up 20% and then down 20%, it returns to the original price.
misconceptions.why: Students see the same percent twice and expect the changes to cancel, forgetting that the second percent uses a new starting amount.
misconceptions.fix: Calculate each step in dollars. Draw two tape diagrams, one for the original amount and one for the new amount, and compare what 20% means in each.

errorCase.story: A game costs 50 dollars. The price rises 20% and later falls 20%.
steps: 20% of 50 is 10, so the price rises to 50 + 10 = 60 dollars.
20% of 60 is 12, so the price falls to 60 − 12 = 48 dollars.
The price is back to 50 dollars.
errorCase.explain: The second 20% is taken from 60 dollars, not from 50 dollars, so the final price is 48 dollars. The percents are equal, but the amounts they come from are different.

misconceptions.belief: A 30% discount means subtract 30 dollars.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the percent sign as a label on the number and subtract the number itself from the price.
misconceptions.fix: Say 30% of the price first, then calculate it. Use a tape diagram cut into ten equal parts and shade three of them.

errorCase.story: A jacket costs 80 dollars and is on sale for 30% off.
steps: The jacket costs 80 dollars and the discount is 30%.
Subtract: 80 − 30 = 50 dollars.
errorCase.explain: 30% of 80 is 0.30 × 80 = 24, not 30. The sale price is 80 − 24 = 56 dollars.

misconceptions.belief: To find percent change, divide the change by the new amount.
misconceptions.why: Students divide by whichever number they see last, which is often the new amount.
misconceptions.fix: Ask what the percent compares to. A percent change always compares to the starting amount, so the original goes on the bottom.

errorCase.story: A bike helmet price rises from 20 dollars to 25 dollars.
steps: The price went up 25 − 20 = 5 dollars.
The percent change is 5 ÷ 25 = 20%.
So the price rose by 20%.
errorCase.explain: The change is compared to the original amount, 20 dollars. 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, so the price rose by 25%.

misconceptions.belief: The phrase '40% more than 50' means 40% of 50.
misconceptions.why: The words more than are skipped, so students find the percent but forget to add it to the original amount.
misconceptions.fix: Act out the phrase with two steps: find 40% of 50, which is 20, then add it to 50 to get 70. Compare with the phrase '40% of 50'.

reading.title: Price Tags at the Sports Shop
reading.text: Marcus works at the Parkview Sports Shop, and he checks the price tags. A pair of cleats has an original amount of 60 dollars. The shop gives a 25% discount, which is 15 dollars, so the sale price is 45 dollars. A backpack used to cost 40 dollars and now costs 46 dollars. The price went up by 6 dollars, and 6 is 15% of 40, so the percent change is an increase of 15%. The shop buys a ball for 8 dollars and adds a markup of 50% of that cost, which is 4 dollars, so customers pay 12 dollars. Marcus sees that every percent is taken from a starting amount. A 25% discount on 60 dollars is not the same as 25% of 45 dollars.
reading.simple: Marcus works at a sports shop. Cleats have an original amount of 60 dollars. A 25% discount is 15 dollars, so the sale price is 45 dollars. A backpack cost 40 dollars and now costs 46 dollars. The price went up 6 dollars, and 6 is 15% of 40. The percent change is 15%. A ball costs the shop 8 dollars. A markup of 50% is 4 dollars, so customers pay 12 dollars. A 25% discount on 60 dollars is not the same as 25% of 45 dollars.

questions.q: What is the sale price of the cleats?
questions.a: 45 dollars

questions.q: Why is a 25% discount on 60 dollars different from 25% of 45 dollars?
questions.a: The percent is taken from a different starting amount: 25% of 60 is 15, but 25% of 45 is less.

questions.q: The backpack price rose from 40 dollars to 46 dollars. How do you know the increase is 15%?
questions.a: The change is 6 dollars, and 6 ÷ 40 = 0.15, which is 15%.

wdntb.why: The first three each equal 10. 50 − 20 equals 30, because it subtracts the percent number instead of finding a part of 50.

noticeWonder.prompt: A jacket tag says 80 dollars. A sign says 25% off and a second tag says 60 dollars. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: To find a percent of an amount, you can multiply the amount by the percent written as a decimal.
asn.why: A percent means per hundred, so 35% is 0.35 and 35% of any amount is 0.35 times that amount.

asn.claim: A 10% increase followed by a 10% decrease returns to the starting amount.
asn.why: The decrease is taken from the larger new amount. For 100 dollars, up 10% is 110 and down 10% is 99.

wyr.q: Would you rather get 20% off an 80 dollar item or 15 dollars off the same item?

compare.a: Kai finds 30% of 80 by calculating 0.30 × 80 = 24 and then subtracts 80 − 24.
compare.b: Lena finds the sale price directly as 70% of 80, so 0.70 × 80 = 56.
compare.prompt: Do both strategies give the same sale price? Why does Lena's shortcut work?

debate.claim: A 50% discount followed by another 50% discount makes an item free.
debate.forEvidence: Fifty percent and fifty percent add up to 100%, so it seems nothing is left.
debate.againstEvidence: The second 50% is taken from what remains: an 80 dollar item drops to 40 dollars and then to 20 dollars.

listening.script: Listen to Ana plan a school fundraiser. We buy T-shirts for 12 dollars each, and we want a markup of 25%. Twenty-five percent of 12 is 3, so we sell each shirt for 15 dollars. Then the principal says to add 8% sales tax. Eight percent of 15 dollars is 1 dollar and 20 cents, so a customer pays 16 dollars and 20 cents. A friend says we should add 25 and 8 and take 33% of 12. But the tax is figured on the selling price, not on the cost, so that plan gives a different answer.

tasks.q: How much does a customer pay for one shirt, including tax?
tasks.why: The selling price is 12 + 3 = 15 dollars. Tax is 8% of 15, which is 1.20, so the total is 16.20 dollars.

tasks.q: Why does the friend's plan give a different answer?
options: Tax is figured on the selling price, which is a different starting amount than the cost.
tasks.why: 33% of 12 is 3.96, which gives 15.96 dollars. The real total is 16.20 dollars because the tax comes from 15 dollars.

story.title: The Spirit Store Price List
story.goal: set prices that cover costs and still look fair to shoppers
story.intro: Lucia manages the spirit store for the student council. Every item has a cost, and she wants a price list that earns a little money without scaring shoppers away.

beats.lead: Lucia reads the cost of the first item and decides how much markup to add.
beats.success: She finds the markup as a percent of the cost, and the new price makes sense.
beats.redirect: The price looks off, so Lucia checks which amount her percent was taken from.

beats.lead: The council asks for a sale sign at the end of the month.
beats.success: Lucia takes the discount from the selling price, and the sale price stays above the cost.
beats.redirect: The sale price is below the cost, so Lucia rechecks the amount her discount came from.

beats.lead: A shopper asks how much the price changed from last year.
beats.success: Lucia divides the change by last year's price and explains the percent change clearly.
beats.redirect: The percent seems too small, so Lucia checks which price she divided by.

story.ending: The sale is a success, and Lucia can explain every percent on the price list.

panels.says: The library book sale takes 40% off every price.
So an atlas that cost 30 dollars now costs 30 − 40 dollars?
No. Forty percent is a part of 30 dollars, so find 40% of 30 first.
Forty percent of 30 is 12, so I save 12 dollars and pay 18 dollars.

predict.q: A calculator costs 50 dollars and is 30% off. Before Noor answers, predict the sale price.
predict.why: 30% of 50 is 15, so the sale price is 50 − 15 = 35 dollars.

transfer.relationship: The new amount is the original amount multiplied by one minus the percent, written as a decimal
phrasings: The sale price is 80% of the original price
new price = 0.80 × original price
A 50 dollar item with 20% off costs 40 dollars
new price = original price − 0.20 × original price

decoys.text: The sale price is 20% of the original price
decoys.why: This keeps only 20% of the price, but 20% off keeps 80%.
This subtracts the percent number as dollars instead of taking 20% of the original price.

modeling.title: Pricing the class shirts
modeling.scenario: A fictional class club sells spirit shirts. The shirts cost the club 20 dollars each, and the club adds a markup and later runs an end-of-season sale.
assumptions: Every shirt costs the club exactly 20 dollars.
The discount is taken from the marked-up price.
Sales tax is ignored.
prompts: What is the selling price after a 30% markup on a 20 dollar cost?
What is the sale price after 20% off the selling price?
Does the club still earn money on each shirt at the sale price? How much on 50 shirts?
limits: Real shops also pay for storage and printing, which are not counted here.
Shoppers might buy more or fewer shirts when the price changes.

sentence.base: A 20% discount on a 50 dollar item leaves a price of 40 dollars.
sentence.because: A 20% discount on a 50 dollar item leaves 40 dollars because 20% of 50 is 10 and 50 minus 10 is 40.
sentence.but: A 20% discount sounds small, but it takes 10 dollars off a 50 dollar item.
sentence.so: The discount is 10 dollars, so the sale price is 40 dollars.

diagnostic.prompt: A pair of shoes costs 50 dollars and is on sale for 30% off. Find the sale price and tell which amount the 30% was taken from.
lookFor: Finds 30% of 50 as 15 dollars
Subtracts to get a sale price of 35 dollars, or multiplies by 70%
Names the original price as the amount the percent was taken from
diagnostic.language: Let the student draw a tape diagram of the price and shade the discount before explaining. If the drawing is right, the barrier is the vocabulary of the sale, not the percent.

extension.task: A store marks up a 20 dollar item by 50% and then takes 50% off the new price. Find the final price and compare it with the cost.
extension.reasoning: Write an argument that explains why the final price is not 20 dollars, using the amount each 50% was taken from.

en.learning: Your child is learning to solve real percent problems, like finding a sale price or a tip, and to say which amount the percent comes from.
en.say: A percent is always a part of some starting amount. Ask first: percent of what?
en.ask: A 40 dollar shirt is 25% off. How much do you save, and what do you pay?
en.activity: Look at a sale flyer or a restaurant bill together. Ask your child to find one discount or tip and explain each step.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a resolver problemas reales de porcentajes, como hallar un precio de oferta o una propina, y a decir de qué cantidad se toma el porcentaje.
es.say: Un porcentaje siempre es una parte de una cantidad inicial. Pregunten primero: ¿el porcentaje de qué?
es.ask: Una camisa de 40 dólares tiene 25% de descuento. ¿Cuánto ahorran y cuánto pagan?
es.activity: Miren juntos un folleto de ofertas o la cuenta de un restaurante. Pidan a su hijo o hija que halle un descuento o una propina y que explique cada paso.

skills.objective: Students add, subtract, multiply and divide positive and negative integers, fractions and decimals, and describe the sign and size of each result using a number line and the properties of operations.
skills.studentObjective: I can add, subtract, multiply and divide positive and negative numbers and explain why the answer has its sign.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain a calculation with negative numbers using because, but and so with the words opposite, absolute value and difference.
successCriteria: I show addition and subtraction of rational numbers as moves on a number line.
I rewrite subtracting a number as adding its opposite.
I give the sign of a product or quotient and explain why.
I say what the sign and the absolute value of an answer mean in the situation.
skills.bigIdea: The sign of a rational number tells direction and its absolute value tells size, so every operation can be explained as movement and distance on a number line.

syntax: Subtracting ___ is the same as adding its opposite, ___.
The answer is negative because ___ and ___ have different signs.
discourse: Describe a change on a number line in order
Justify the sign of an answer with a pattern or a model

domains.listening: Students listen to a game score story and track each gain and loss on a number line.

errorCase.story: The high temperature is 4 degrees and the low is −6 degrees.
steps: The high is 4 degrees and the low is −6 degrees.
The difference is 4 − (−6) = 4 − 6 = −2 degrees.
errorCase.explain: Subtracting −6 means adding its opposite: 4 + 6 = 10. The difference is 10 degrees, the distance from −6 up to 4.

misconceptions.belief: A product of two negative numbers is negative.
misconceptions.why: Students link the word negative with the answer, and a negative sign in the problem seems to carry into the result.
misconceptions.fix: Build a pattern: (−5) × 3, (−5) × 2, (−5) × 1, (−5) × 0, and keep going. Ask what number must come next each time.

errorCase.story: Dani multiplies two negative numbers.
steps: The sizes multiply to 5 × 3 = 15.
Both numbers are negative, so the product must be negative: (−5) × (−3) = −15.
errorCase.explain: Factors with the same sign give a positive product. The pattern (−5) × 1 = −5, (−5) × 0 = 0, (−5) × (−1) = 5 keeps growing, so (−5) × (−3) = 15.

misconceptions.belief: To add numbers with different signs, add their sizes and keep the sign of the first number.
misconceptions.why: Adding is learned with positive numbers, so students keep adding and only look at the first sign.
misconceptions.fix: Move on a number line: start at the first number, then move right for a positive number and left for a negative one.

errorCase.story: A bank account is at −8 dollars and then 5 dollars is deposited.
steps: The account starts at −8 dollars.
A deposit adds 5 dollars, so −8 + 5 = −13 dollars.
errorCase.explain: A deposit moves the balance 5 to the right: from −8 to −3. The account is still in debt, but by 3 dollars, not 13.

misconceptions.belief: The difference between 4 and −6 is 2.
misconceptions.why: The word difference sounds like a comparison of sizes, so students subtract 6 − 4 and ignore that the numbers lie on opposite sides of zero.
misconceptions.fix: Place both numbers on a number line and count the distance between them. Say how many units apart before writing a number sentence.

reading.title: A Cold Night at the Weather Station
reading.text: Luis and Amira study the weather for their science club. At midnight the temperature is −3.5 degrees Celsius. By 6 a.m. it drops another 2.5 degrees, so the new temperature is −3.5 + (−2.5) = −6 degrees. The absolute value of −6 is 6, because −6 is 6 units from zero. At noon the temperature reaches 4 degrees. To find the difference between the high and the low, Luis subtracts 4 − (−6) = 10 degrees. Amira notices that subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its opposite. If the temperature fell 1.5 degrees each hour for 4 hours, the total change was 4 × (−1.5) = −6 degrees. The sign of an answer tells the direction of the change.
reading.simple: Luis and Amira study the weather. At midnight the temperature is −3.5 degrees. By 6 a.m. it drops 2.5 degrees. So −3.5 + (−2.5) = −6 degrees. The absolute value of −6 is 6. At noon the temperature is 4 degrees. The difference between the high and the low is 4 − (−6) = 10 degrees. Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its opposite. If the temperature fell 1.5 degrees each hour for 4 hours, the change was 4 × (−1.5) = −6 degrees.

questions.q: What is the temperature at 6 a.m.?
questions.a: −6 degrees

questions.q: Why does Luis get 10 degrees for the difference even though one temperature is negative?
questions.a: Subtracting −6 is the same as adding 6, and the two temperatures are 10 units apart on the number line.

questions.q: What is the product 4 × (−1.5), and what does the negative sign tell you?
questions.a: −6; the temperature went down.

wdntb.why: The first three equal 5. −3 − 8 equals −11, because it moves 8 more units to the left of −3.

My friend says I should be at negative 13, because she added the sizes 9 and 4. But taking away a penalty should help my score, not hurt it. Moving 4 up from negative 9 lands at negative 5.

reading.title: The Bracelet Table
reading.text: Jonas sells bracelets at the school fair. Each bracelet sells for 4 dollars, and he pays 9 dollars for a table. If x is the number of bracelets he sells, the expression 4x − 9 shows his profit. The coefficient 4 is the price of one bracelet. Jonas wants a profit of 31 dollars, so he writes the equation 4x − 9 = 31. He uses inverse operations: adding 9 to both sides gives 4x = 40, and dividing both sides by 4 gives x = 10. His friend Tali sells bead kits and writes the expression 2(x + 3). She says it is equivalent to 2x + 6. They test x = 4: 2(4 + 3) = 14 and 2(4) + 6 = 14. The expressions match for every value of x, because multiplying 2 by both terms inside the parentheses gives 2x + 6.
reading.simple: Jonas sells bracelets for 4 dollars each, and he pays 9 dollars for a table. If x is the number of bracelets, the expression 4x − 9 shows his profit. Jonas wants a profit of 31 dollars, so he solves 4x − 9 = 31. He adds 9 to both sides to get 4x = 40. Then he divides by 4 and gets x = 10. Tali says 2(x + 3) is equivalent to 2x + 6. questions.q: Why does Jonas add 9 to both sides of the equation?

misconceptions.belief: When you divide both sides by a negative number, the inequality symbol stays the same.
misconceptions.why: Equations never change direction, so students carry the same habit to inequalities.
misconceptions.fix: Test two numbers on each side of the boundary in the original inequality. Then see which numbers work and which direction the symbol must point.

errorCase.story: Omar solves −2x > 10.
steps: Divide both sides by −2.
So x > −5.
errorCase.explain: Dividing by a negative number reverses the symbol, so x < −5. Check x = −6: −2(−6) = 12, which is greater than 10. Check x = −4: −2(−4) = 8, which is not.

misconceptions.belief: 'At least 12' means greater than 12, without 12.
misconceptions.why: In everyday speech at least sounds like more, so students drop the boundary number.
misconceptions.fix: Act out a real limit, such as a bus that needs at least 12 riders, and ask whether exactly 12 riders is enough.

errorCase.story: A school bus needs at least 12 riders to run.
steps: The bus needs at least 12 riders.
So the number of riders r must satisfy r > 12.
Exactly 12 riders is not enough.
errorCase.explain: At least 12 includes 12, so the inequality is r ≥ 12. With exactly 12 riders the bus runs.

misconceptions.belief: The inequality 8 > x says that x is greater than 8.
misconceptions.why: Students read the symbol as pointing at the number it opens toward, or read left to right and attach greater than to the variable.
misconceptions.fix: Read it aloud as 8 is greater than x, then flip it so the variable comes first: x < 8. Test with x = 3 and x = 12.

misconceptions.belief: 'At most 17' means 17 or more.
misconceptions.why: The word most sounds like a large number, so students attach it to the greater values.
misconceptions.fix: Use a real limit, such as a pack that can hold at most 12 kilograms. Ask whether 15 kilograms fits.

reading.title: Markers and Car Washes
reading.text: Devon has 40 dollars for art supplies. A sketchbook costs 6 dollars and each marker costs 2 dollars. If m is the number of markers, the constraint is the inequality 6 + 2m ≤ 40. Subtracting 6 from both sides gives 2m ≤ 34, and dividing by 2 gives m ≤ 17. The solution set includes every number of markers that is 17 or fewer, so Devon can buy at most 17 markers. His friend Lila is raising money at a car wash. She needs at least 50 dollars and earns 5 dollars for each car, so 5c ≥ 50 and c ≥ 10. Ten cars is allowed, so the circle on the number line for 10 is filled in. If the goal were more than 50 dollars, the inequality would be 5c > 50, and 10 cars would not be enough.
reading.simple: Devon has 40 dollars. A sketchbook costs 6 dollars and each marker costs 2 dollars. The inequality is 6 + 2m ≤ 40. Subtract 6 to get 2m ≤ 34. Divide by 2 to get m ≤ 17. The solution set is 17 or fewer markers. Lila needs at least 50 dollars and earns 5 dollars for each car, so 5c ≥ 50 and c ≥ 10. Ten cars is enough, so the circle for 10 is filled in. For more than 50 dollars, 5c > 50 and 10 cars is not enough.

questions.q: How much does each marker cost?
questions.a: 2 dollars

questions.q: Why is the circle at 10 filled in for Lila's goal but not for a goal of more than 50 dollars?
questions.a: At least 50 dollars allows exactly 50, so 10 cars is a solution. More than 50 does not allow 50, so 10 cars is not a solution.

questions.q: Show that 17 markers fit in Devon's budget.
questions.a: 6 + 2 × 17 = 6 + 34 = 40, which is not more than 40.

wdntb.why: x < 5 leaves out the number 5. The other three all say that x is 5 or less, including 5.

noticeWonder.prompt: One number line shows a filled circle at 10 with an arrow pointing right. Another shows an open circle at 10 with an arrow pointing right. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: Multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality symbol.
asn.why: Negative numbers reverse the order on the number line, so 2 < 5 becomes −2 > −5.

asn.claim: The solution set of an inequality has a greatest number in it.
asn.why: The set m ≤ 17 has 17 as its greatest number, but x < 17 over all rational numbers has none, because there is always a number closer to 17.

wyr.q: Would you rather show the limit 6 + 2m ≤ 40 as a number line graph or as a sentence with at most?

compare.a: Pia solves 3x − 5 > 10 by adding 5 to get 3x > 15 and dividing by 3 to get x > 5.
compare.b: Quin tests numbers: x = 5 gives 3(5) − 5 = 10, which is not more than 10, and x = 6 gives 13, which is more.
compare.prompt: Which strategy proves the whole solution set? What does testing numbers add?

debate.claim: 'At most 12' and 'less than 12' mean the same thing.
debate.forEvidence: Both phrases talk about numbers that are not bigger than 12.
debate.againstEvidence: At most 12 includes 12 itself, but less than 12 does not, so exactly 12 kilograms is allowed only by the first phrase.

listening.script: Listen to Rosa plan a hiking day. My pack can hold at most 12 kilograms. The empty pack weighs 2 kilograms, and each water bottle weighs 1.5 kilograms. If w is the number of bottles, then 2 plus 1.5w must be at most 12. Subtracting 2 from both sides gives 1.5w is at most 10. Dividing by 1.5, w is at most six and two thirds. But you cannot carry part of a bottle, so I pack 6 bottles. Check: 6 bottles weigh 9 kilograms, and 2 plus 9 is 11, under the limit. Seven bottles would make 12 and a half kilograms, which is too heavy.

tasks.q: How many water bottles does Rosa pack?
tasks.why: w ≤ 6 2/3, and bottles come in whole numbers, so the greatest number is 6.

tasks.q: Why does Rosa not pack 7 bottles?
options: Seven bottles make the pack weigh 12.5 kilograms, which is over the limit.
The pack must always weigh less than 11 kilograms.
tasks.why: 2 + 1.5 × 7 = 12.5, which is more than 12.

story.title: The Lane Rope Fund
story.goal: raise enough money for new lane ropes without going over the budget
story.intro: Hana volunteers at the community pool. The pool needs new lane ropes, and Hana must keep spending under a fixed limit while she raises a minimum amount.

beats.lead: Hana reads the limit on the order form and turns the sentence into an inequality.
beats.success: Her inequality uses the right symbol, and she explains whether the boundary is allowed.
beats.redirect: The symbol leaves out a number that should be allowed, so Hana rereads the phrase at most.

beats.lead: The team solves the inequality to find how many ropes they can order.
beats.success: They undo the operations in order and keep the symbol facing the right way.
beats.redirect: The answer does not fit when they test a number, so they check the last step.

beats.lead: Hana draws the solution on a number line for the poster.
beats.success: The filled circle and the arrow match the inequality, and visitors read it easily.
beats.redirect: The arrow points the wrong way, so Hana tests a number from the shaded side.

story.ending: The pool orders the ropes within budget, and Hana can explain every number that works.

panels.says: Our robot needs at least 18 points to reach the next round.
We have 6 points and each challenge gives 4, so 6 + 4c ≥ 18.
Subtract 6 to get 4c ≥ 12, so c ≥ 3.
Check it: 3 challenges give 6 + 12 = 18, which is exactly enough.

predict.q: Before Carla checks, predict how many challenges are enough for the next round.
predict.why: 4c ≥ 12 gives c ≥ 3, and exactly 3 challenges reach 18 points.

transfer.relationship: A fixed amount plus a repeated amount must stay at or below a limit
phrasings: Devon can buy at most 17 markers
A filled circle at 17 on a number line, with the shading going left
A 6 dollar sketchbook plus 2 dollars per marker may not go over 40 dollars

decoys.why: Seventeen markers cost exactly 40 dollars, which is allowed, but this symbol leaves 17 out.

decoys.text: A filled circle at 17 with the shading going right
decoys.why: This would allow 20 markers, which cost 46 dollars and go over the budget.

modeling.title: Planning a field trip budget
modeling.scenario: A fictional class is planning a field trip with a limited budget. The bus costs a flat amount and each student needs a ticket.
assumptions: Every student who goes needs one ticket.
The bus rental is paid once.
The class cannot spend more than the budget.
prompts: Write an inequality for the number of tickets t and solve it for the 8 dollar ticket.
Can all 22 students go? Explain with your solution set.
The ticket price rises to 9 dollars. How many students can go now?
limits: Real trips may have extra fees, like food, that are not counted here.
Students might need adult tickets that cost more.

sentence.because: The solution to 6 + 2m ≤ 40 is m ≤ 17 because 2m ≤ 34 after subtracting 6, and 34 ÷ 2 is 17.
sentence.but: Devon cannot buy 17.5 markers, but every whole number up to 17 works.
sentence.so: Seventeen markers cost exactly 40 dollars, so the solution set includes 17.

diagnostic.prompt: A taxi charges 4 dollars plus 3 dollars for each mile. Mia has at most 25 dollars. Write and solve an inequality, graph it, and tell what the solution set means.
lookFor: Writes 4 + 3m ≤ 25 and solves to m ≤ 7
Graphs a filled circle at 7 with shading to the left
Says Mia can ride up to 7 miles, including exactly 7
diagnostic.language: Let the student sort the cost for 5, 7 and 8 miles on a number line before writing a sentence. If the sorting is correct, the barrier is the words at most, not the inequality.

extension.task: Solve −3x + 5 ≥ −10 and graph the solution set. Then pick two numbers from the graph and check them in the original inequality.
extension.reasoning: Explain why the inequality symbol reverses when you divide by −3, using test values on both sides of the boundary.

en.learning: Your child is learning to use inequalities to describe limits and goals, like having at most 20 dollars to spend or needing at least 10 points.
en.say: At most means that number or fewer. At least means that number or more.
en.ask: You have 20 dollars and each slice of pizza costs 3 dollars. What is the greatest number of slices you can buy?
en.activity: Pick a small budget at the store. Ask your child to say how many of an item you can buy without going over, and to explain how they know.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a usar desigualdades para describir límites y metas, como tener a lo sumo 20 dólares para gastar o necesitar al menos 10 puntos.
es.say: A lo sumo significa ese número o menos. Al menos significa ese número o más.
es.ask: Tienen 20 dólares y cada porción de pizza cuesta 3 dólares. ¿Cuál es el mayor número de porciones que pueden comprar?

skills.objective: Students use a scale to find actual lengths from a scale drawing, to draw lengths at a different scale, and to explain the scale as a constant ratio between drawing and actual lengths.
skills.studentObjective: I can use a scale to find real lengths from a drawing and to draw real objects at a smaller size.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how a scale works using because, but and so with the words scale drawing, scale factor and corresponding sides.
successCriteria: I read a scale and write it as a ratio with matching units.
I find an actual length from a drawing length and a drawing length from an actual length.
I check that all corresponding sides use the same scale factor.
I explain in a full sentence what one unit on the drawing stands for.
skills.bigIdea: A scale drawing keeps every length in the same ratio to the real length, so the drawing has the same shape as the real object.

syntax: On the drawing, 1 ___ stands for ___ in real life.
The actual length is ___ because I multiplied the drawing length by ___.
discourse: Explain a map or plan to someone who has not seen it
Justify whether to multiply or divide by the scale

domains.listening: Students listen to a trail map description and mark the distances on a simple map.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner what one centimeter on the drawing stands for and how they used it.
domains.reading: Students read a short garden plan report and match each drawing length to its actual length.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about a scale drawing.

vocab.def: A drawing whose lengths all have the same ratio to the real lengths.
vocab.example: A plan where 1 centimeter stands for 2 meters of garden
vocab.nonExample: A sketch drawn by eye with no measuring
vocab.sentence: The class draws a scale drawing of the school garden.

vocab.def: The number that every real length is multiplied or divided by to get the drawing length.
vocab.example: 200, when 1 centimeter on the drawing stands for 200 centimeters
vocab.nonExample: The number of sides on the shape
vocab.sentence: One centimeter stands for 200 centimeters, so the scale factor is 200.

vocab.def: The ratio that compares a length on a drawing with the real length.
vocab.example: 1 centimeter to 2 meters
vocab.nonExample: A bathroom scale that tells your weight
vocab.sentence: The scale of the garden plan is 1 centimeter to 2 meters.
vocab.everyday: A tool that tells how heavy something is

vocab.def: The real measure of an object, not the size shown in the drawing.
vocab.example: The garden is 12 meters long
vocab.nonExample: The garden is 6 centimeters long on the drawing
vocab.sentence: Imani multiplies to find the actual length of the garden.

vocab.def: Sides in the same position in two figures that have the same shape.
vocab.example: The 6 centimeter side on the plan and the 12 meter side of the garden
vocab.nonExample: The 6 centimeter side and the 8 meter side, which are in different positions
vocab.sentence: Corresponding sides use the same scale.
vocab.morphology: co- means together; respond means to answer back

misconceptions.belief: To find an actual length, add the scale number to the drawing length.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the scale as a number to combine with the drawing length and not as a repeated ratio.
misconceptions.fix: Build a table: 1 cm is 3 m, 2 cm is 6 m, 3 cm is 9 m. Ask what happens to the real length each time the drawing length goes up by 1.

errorCase.story: A scale drawing uses 1 centimeter for every 3 meters, and a pool is 5 centimeters long on the drawing.
steps: The scale is 1 centimeter to 3 meters.
Add: 5 + 3 = 8, so the pool is 8 meters long.
errorCase.explain: Every centimeter stands for 3 meters, so multiply: 5 × 3 = 15 meters.

misconceptions.belief: To find a drawing length from an actual length, always multiply by the scale number.
misconceptions.why: Students practice multiplying to find actual lengths, so they multiply again when the direction of the problem reverses.
misconceptions.fix: Ask which length is bigger, the drawing or the real object. A drawing of a large object is smaller than the object, so divide.

errorCase.story: A field is 24 meters long, and the drawing uses 1 centimeter for every 4 meters.
steps: The field is 24 meters long, and 1 centimeter stands for 4 meters.
Multiply: 24 × 4 = 96 centimeters on the drawing.
errorCase.explain: The drawing is smaller than the field, so divide: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 centimeters.

misconceptions.belief: A scale of 1 centimeter to 2 meters is the ratio 1 to 2.
misconceptions.why: Students read the two numbers and ignore the units, so they do not notice that centimeters and meters are different sizes.
misconceptions.fix: Write both quantities in the same unit first: 1 centimeter to 200 centimeters, then read the ratio.

errorCase.story: A model plane uses a scale of 1 centimeter to 2 meters.
steps: The scale is 1 centimeter to 2 meters, which is the ratio 1 to 2.
So the real plane is 2 times as long as the model.
errorCase.explain: Two meters is 200 centimeters, so in the same unit the ratio is 1 to 200. The real plane is 200 times as long as the model.

misconceptions.belief: If every length is multiplied by 3, the area is also multiplied by 3.
misconceptions.why: Students extend the idea that every measure grows by the scale factor without picturing two directions of growth.
misconceptions.fix: Draw a 2 by 2 square and a 6 by 6 square on grid paper, count the unit squares, and compare the areas.

reading.title: A Plan of the School Garden
reading.text: Imani's class draws a scale drawing of the school garden. The scale is 1 centimeter to 2 meters. On the drawing, the garden is 6 centimeters long and 4 centimeters wide. To find the actual length, Imani multiplies 6 by 2 and gets 12 meters. The actual width is 4 × 2 = 8 meters. A path along one side is 10 meters long in the garden, so Imani draws it 5 centimeters long, because 10 ÷ 2 = 5. Corresponding sides of the drawing and the garden are in the same ratio, which is why the drawing has the same shape. Tomas says the scale means the garden is 2 times as big as the drawing, but that mixes up the units. One centimeter on paper stands for 200 centimeters in the garden, so the scale factor is 200.
reading.simple: Imani's class draws a scale drawing of the school garden. The scale is 1 centimeter to 2 meters. On the drawing the garden is 6 centimeters long and 4 centimeters wide. The actual length is 6 × 2 = 12 meters. The actual width is 4 × 2 = 8 meters. A path is 10 meters long, so Imani draws it 5 centimeters long, because 10 ÷ 2 = 5. Tomas says the garden is 2 times as big as the drawing, but that mixes up the units. One centimeter stands for 200 centimeters.

questions.q: How wide is the garden in real life?
questions.a: 8 meters

questions.q: Why is Tomas wrong when he says the garden is 2 times as big as the drawing?
questions.a: He compares centimeters with meters. In the same unit, 1 centimeter stands for 200 centimeters, so the garden is 200 times as big.

questions.q: How long does Imani draw the 10 meter path, and what calculation gives that?
questions.a: 5 centimeters, from 10 ÷ 2.

wdntb.why: The first three each stand for 2 meters per centimeter. 1 cm : 3 m stands for 3 meters per centimeter.

noticeWonder.prompt: A map shows the library 3 centimeters from the park, and the key says 1 centimeter equals 5 kilometers. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If a scale drawing makes every length twice as long, the new drawing has the same shape as the original.
asn.why: All corresponding sides are multiplied by the same factor, so the shape stays the same and only the size changes.

asn.claim: A scale drawing shows the object smaller than it really is.
asn.why: A map of a town is smaller than the town, but a drawing of an insect enlarged to fill a page is larger than the insect.

wyr.q: Would you rather find a missing length with a double number line or by multiplying by the scale?

compare.a: Kia draws a double number line with 0, 1, 2, 3 centimeters above 0, 2, 4, 6 meters and reads that 3 centimeters is 6 meters.
compare.b: Leo multiplies the drawing length by the scale: 3 × 2 = 6 meters.
compare.prompt: Do both strategies give the same actual length? How are they connected?

debate.claim: A scale of 1 centimeter to 2 meters means the real object is 2 times as long as the drawing.
debate.forEvidence: The scale has a 2 in it, so the real object seems to be 2 times as long.
debate.againstEvidence: Two meters is 200 centimeters, so in the same unit the real object is 200 times as long as the drawing.

listening.script: Listen to Marco explain a map of a hiking trail. The scale is 1 inch for every 5 miles. The lake is 3 inches from the cabin on the map. To find the real distance, I multiply 3 by 5 and get 15 miles. Next, the ranger station is 20 miles from the cabin. To place it on the map, I divide 20 by 5, so it is 4 inches from the cabin. My cousin says to add, 20 plus 5. That would put the station 25 inches away, and it would fall off the page.

tasks.q: How far from the cabin is the ranger station on the map?
tasks.why: 20 miles ÷ 5 miles per inch = 4 inches.

tasks.q: What is wrong with adding 5 to 20?
options: Each inch stands for 5 miles, so the real distance is divided by 5, not added to.
Twenty is too big a number to use on a map.
Maps cannot show distances in miles.
tasks.why: A scale is a ratio, so you multiply or divide. Adding mixes up miles and inches.

story.title: The Reading Garden Plan
story.goal: plan a reading garden to scale before anyone digs
story.intro: Dara helps the library plan a small reading garden. She draws it on paper first, because every bench and path must fit on the lawn.

beats.lead: Dara reads the scale on her plan and measures the first bench on paper.
beats.success: She multiplies by the scale and gets the actual length of the bench.
beats.redirect: The bench seems far too big, so Dara checks which direction her calculation goes.

beats.lead: The librarian wants a path of a certain real length to be added to the plan.
beats.success: Dara divides by the scale and draws the path at the right length.
beats.redirect: The path runs off the page, so Dara checks whether she multiplied or divided.

beats.lead: A neighbor asks if the plan keeps the shape of the lawn.
beats.success: Dara shows that corresponding sides use the same scale and explains why the shape holds.
beats.redirect: One side looks off, so Dara measures both sides again and compares the scale factor.

story.ending: The reading garden fits the lawn perfectly, and Dara can explain what every centimeter on the plan stands for.

panels.says: My model bridge is 9 centimeters long, and the scale is 1 centimeter to 4 meters.
So the real bridge is 9 × 4 = 36 meters long.
Right. The real tower is 28 meters tall. How tall should the model tower be?
The model is smaller, so I divide: 28 ÷ 4 = 7 centimeters.

predict.q: A real flagpole is 20 meters tall. Before Jun answers, predict how tall it is on Ayla's model.
predict.why: The model is smaller than the real object, so divide: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 centimeters.

transfer.relationship: Every actual length is the same multiple of its drawing length
phrasings: On the plan, 1 centimeter stands for 2 meters
actual length in meters = 2 × drawing length in centimeters
A table where 3 cm is 6 m, 5 cm is 10 m and 6 cm is 12 m
A double number line with 0, 1, 2, 3 centimeters above 0, 2, 4, 6 meters

decoys.text: actual length in meters = drawing length in centimeters + 2
decoys.why: This adds 2 instead of multiplying, so the real length would not grow in step with the drawing.

decoys.text: actual length in meters = drawing length in centimeters ÷ 2
decoys.why: This divides, so it gives half the drawing length, but each centimeter stands for 2 meters.

modeling.title: Planning a stage on paper
modeling.scenario: A fictional school drama club plans a stage layout on paper. The real stage is large, so the club draws it at a smaller scale to fit on one sheet.
assumptions: The scale is the same for every length on the plan.
The stage is a perfect rectangle.
The table is a straight rectangle.
prompts: How wide and how deep is the stage on the drawing? Show each unit conversion.
Does the drawing fit on the paper? Explain.
How long is the table on the drawing?
limits: A real stage may have curved edges, which a rectangle does not show.
Paper drawings are measured by hand, so small errors can appear.

sentence.base: A scale of 1 centimeter to 4 meters means each centimeter on the drawing stands for 4 meters.
sentence.because: A model bridge 9 centimeters long stands for 36 meters because each centimeter stands for 4 meters.
sentence.but: The model is much smaller than the bridge, but it has the same shape.
sentence.so: Each centimeter stands for 4 meters, so 7 centimeters on the model stands for 28 meters.

diagnostic.prompt: A drawing uses 1 centimeter for 5 meters. A playground is 4 centimeters by 3 centimeters on the drawing. Find the actual size. Then find how long to draw a 35 meter fence.
lookFor: Multiplies to get 20 meters by 15 meters
Divides 35 by 5 to get 7 centimeters for the fence
Labels the units on every number
diagnostic.language: Let the student draw a double number line before using words. If the line is correct, the barrier is the language of scale, not the proportional reasoning.

extension.task: A square garden is 6 centimeters on each side on a drawing with a scale of 1 centimeter to 2 meters. Find the actual area in square meters and the area on the drawing in square centimeters.
extension.reasoning: Explain why the area on the drawing is not simply the actual area divided by 2, using the lengths of the sides.

en.learning: Your child is learning to use a scale on maps and plans, like 1 inch standing for 10 miles, to find real lengths and to draw real objects smaller.
en.say: Each unit on the drawing stands for the same real amount. Multiply to go from the drawing to real life, and divide to go back.
en.ask: On a map, 1 inch stands for 10 miles. Two towns are 4 inches apart. How far apart are they in real life?
en.activity: Look at a map or a floor plan together. Ask your child to pick two places and use the scale to find the real distance.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a usar una escala en mapas y planos, como 1 pulgada que representa 10 millas, para hallar longitudes reales y para dibujar objetos reales más pequeños.
es.say: Cada unidad del dibujo representa la misma cantidad real. Multipliquen para pasar del dibujo a la vida real, y dividan para volver.
es.ask: En un mapa, 1 pulgada representa 10 millas. Dos pueblos están a 4 pulgadas de distancia. ¿A qué distancia están en la vida real?
es.activity: Miren juntos un mapa o un plano de una casa. Pidan a su hijo o hija que escoja dos lugares y que use la escala para hallar la distancia real.

skills.objective: Students find the circumference and area of circles, use supplementary, complementary and vertical angle relationships to find unknown angles, and solve problems about area and volume of simple figures.
skills.studentObjective: I can find the circumference and area of a circle and use angle relationships to find a missing angle.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how I found a measurement using because, but and so with the words circumference, radius and supplementary angles.
successCriteria: I tell the radius from the diameter and use the right one in each formula.
I find the circumference and the area of a circle and name the correct units.
I use supplementary and vertical angles to find a missing angle and explain why.
I say whether an answer measures length around a shape or square units inside it.
skills.bigIdea: Every circle has the same ratio of circumference to diameter, called pi, and angle relationships let us find unknown angles from known ones.

syntax: The circumference is ___ because pi times the diameter is ___.
The two angles are supplementary, so the missing angle is ___.
discourse: Describe the steps of a measurement in order
Explain the difference between length around a shape and area inside it

domains.listening: Students listen to a tablecloth plan and decide which measurement is the ribbon and which is the fabric.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner whether a measurement uses the radius or the diameter and why.
domains.reading: Students read a short garden plan and mark each measurement and its unit.

vocab.def: The distance around a circle.
vocab.example: A flower bed 10 meters across has a circumference of about 31.4 meters
vocab.nonExample: The space inside the circle, which is its area
vocab.sentence: Eli measures the circumference to buy a border.
vocab.morphology: circum- means around; ferre means to carry

vocab.def: The distance from the center of a circle to any point on the circle.
vocab.example: 5 meters, in a circle with a diameter of 10 meters
vocab.nonExample: A segment across the whole circle through the center, which is the diameter
vocab.sentence: The radius of the flower bed is 5 meters.

vocab.def: The distance across a circle through its center; it is twice the radius.
vocab.example: 10 meters, in a circle with a radius of 5 meters
vocab.nonExample: The distance from the center to the edge, which is the radius
vocab.sentence: The diameter of the flower bed is 10 meters.
vocab.morphology: dia- means across; meter means measure

vocab.def: The number you get when you divide any circle's circumference by its diameter, about 3.14.
vocab.example: 3.14, or the fraction 22/7 as an approximation
vocab.nonExample: A pie, a baked dish with a crust, which sounds the same
vocab.sentence: The circumference is pi times the diameter.
vocab.everyday: Sounds like pie, a baked dish with a crust

vocab.def: The number of square units that cover a flat shape.
vocab.example: 78.5 square meters of soil in the flower bed
vocab.nonExample: The distance around the bed, which is its circumference
vocab.sentence: He needs the area to fill the bed with soil.
vocab.everyday: A region or part of a place, like the play area

vocab.def: Two angles whose measures add to 180 degrees.
vocab.example: 50 degrees and 130 degrees
vocab.nonExample: 50 degrees and 40 degrees, which add to 90 degrees
vocab.sentence: Two angles on a straight line are supplementary angles.

misconceptions.belief: In the area formula, r² means r × 2.
misconceptions.why: Students see a small raised 2 and read it as times 2, which is the same shortcut they used in earlier grades for doubling.
misconceptions.fix: Write r² as r × r. Draw a square with side r beside the circle and count how many such squares the circle covers.

errorCase.story: A round rug has a radius of 3 feet.
steps: The radius of the rug is 3 feet.
The area is 3.14 × 3 × 2 = 18.84 square feet.
errorCase.explain: The radius is squared, so use 3 × 3 = 9. The area is 3.14 × 9 = 28.26 square feet.

misconceptions.belief: Supplementary angles add to 90 degrees.
misconceptions.why: Complementary and supplementary sound alike, and students swap the two totals.
misconceptions.fix: Link each word to a picture: a straight line is 180 degrees, a corner is 90 degrees. Use the memory that straight starts with s, like supplementary.

errorCase.story: Two angles lie on a straight line, and one measures 65 degrees.
steps: The two angles lie on a straight line and one measures 65 degrees.
Supplementary angles add to 90 degrees, so the other is 90 − 65 = 25 degrees.
errorCase.explain: Angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees, so the other angle is 180 − 65 = 115 degrees.

misconceptions.belief: Doubling the radius of a circle doubles its area.
misconceptions.why: Students expect every measure of a figure to grow at the same rate as its length.
misconceptions.fix: Compare a circle with radius 2 and one with radius 4 by calculating both areas. Ask how many times larger the second is.

misconceptions.belief: A circle that is 10 meters across has a radius of 10 meters.
misconceptions.why: Students use the only number in the sentence and skip the word across, which describes the diameter.
misconceptions.fix: Mark the measurement on a drawing. Across the whole circle is the diameter, and the radius is half of it.

reading.title: The Round Flower Bed
reading.text: A community garden has a circular flower bed with a diameter of 10 meters, so its radius is 5 meters. Eli wants a border around the edge. The circumference is pi times the diameter, and with pi as 3.14 that is about 31.4 meters. To fill the bed with soil, he needs the area, which is pi times the radius squared: 3.14 × 5 × 5 = 78.5 square meters. Two straight paths cross near the bed. One angle measures 50 degrees. The angle next to it lies on a straight line, so the two are supplementary angles and add to 180 degrees. The next angle is 130 degrees. The angle across from the 50 degree angle is a vertical angle, so it also measures 50 degrees.
reading.simple: A garden has a circular flower bed with a diameter of 10 meters, so its radius is 5 meters. The circumference is pi times the diameter. With pi as 3.14, that is about 31.4 meters. The area is pi times the radius squared: 3.14 × 5 × 5 = 78.5 square meters. Two paths cross near the bed. One angle is 50 degrees. The angle next to it is on a straight line, so they add to 180 degrees. That angle is 130 degrees. The angle across from 50 degrees also measures 50 degrees.

questions.q: What is the radius of the flower bed?
questions.a: 5 meters

questions.q: Why does Eli use circumference for the border and area for the soil?
questions.a: The border goes around the edge, which is a length. The soil covers the whole inside, which is an area.

questions.q: How do you know the angle next to the 50 degree angle is 130 degrees?
questions.a: The two angles are supplementary, so they add to 180, and 180 − 50 = 130.

wdntb.why: The area is measured in square meters because it covers a surface. The other three are lengths measured in meters.

noticeWonder.prompt: A circle with a diameter of 10 has a circumference of 31.4. A circle with a diameter of 20 has a circumference of 62.8. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: The circumference of any circle is a little more than 3 times its diameter.
asn.why: The circumference divided by the diameter is pi for every circle, and pi is about 3.14.

asn.claim: Doubling the radius of a circle doubles its area.
asn.why: Area uses the radius squared, so doubling the radius makes the area four times as large.

wyr.q: Would you rather find a circumference with pi times the diameter or with 2 times pi times the radius?

compare.a: Ola finds the area of a circle with radius 4 as 3.14 × 4 × 4 = 50.24 square units.
compare.b: Pim finds 3.14 × 4 × 2 = 25.12 and says that is the area.
compare.prompt: Whose answer is the area? What does Pim's number actually measure?

debate.claim: If you double a circle's diameter, both its circumference and its area double.
debate.forEvidence: Everything about a circle should grow at the same rate as its width.
debate.againstEvidence: The circumference goes from 31.4 to 62.8, which doubles, but the area goes from 78.5 to 314, which is four times as large.

listening.script: Listen to Paloma plan a round tablecloth. The table is a circle with a diameter of 6 feet. The edge of the cloth needs ribbon all the way around. That distance is the circumference, pi times the diameter, so about 3.14 times 6, or 18.84 feet. Next she wants to know how much fabric covers the top. That is the area. The radius is 3 feet, so the area is 3.14 times 3 times 3, which is 28.26 square feet. The two numbers are different because they measure different things: feet measure the length around, and square feet measure the flat space.

tasks.q: What is the area of the tabletop?
tasks.why: The radius is 3 feet, so the area is 3.14 × 3 × 3 = 28.26 square feet.

tasks.q: Which measurement matches the ribbon around the edge?
tasks.why: The ribbon goes around the edge, and the distance around a circle is its circumference.

story.title: The Courtyard Reading Rug
story.goal: design a round reading rug with trim around the edge
story.intro: Ravi is designing a round rug for the courtyard. The rug needs fabric for the top and trim for the edge, and each one needs a different measurement.

beats.lead: Ravi measures across the rug and decides which measurement he has.
beats.success: He names it the diameter and finds the radius by halving it.
beats.redirect: His radius looks too large, so Ravi checks whether he measured across or from the center.

beats.lead: The trim is sold by the foot, so Ravi needs the distance around the rug.
beats.success: He multiplies pi by the diameter and orders the right length of trim.
beats.redirect: The trim order seems too short, so Ravi checks which formula he used.

beats.lead: The fabric is sold by the square foot, so Ravi needs the space inside the rug.
beats.success: He squares the radius before multiplying by pi and orders the right amount of fabric.
beats.redirect: The fabric order seems too small, so Ravi checks whether he squared the radius.

story.ending: The rug fits the courtyard, and Ravi can explain why the trim and the fabric need different measurements.

panels.says: My circle has a diameter of 14 centimeters. So the radius is 14, right?
No, the radius is half of the diameter. What is it?
Seven centimeters. Now the area is 3.14 × 7 × 7.
Seven times seven is 49, so the area is 3.14 × 49 = 153.86 square centimeters.

predict.q: A different circle has a diameter of 20 centimeters. Before Wren answers, predict its circumference using 3.14.
predict.why: The circumference is pi times the diameter: 3.14 × 20 = 62.8 centimeters.

transfer.relationship: The distance around a circle is always the same multiple of the distance across it, about 3.14
phrasings: The circumference of a circle is about 3.14 times its diameter
C = πd
A circle 10 meters across has an edge about 31.4 meters long
A table where a diameter of 2 gives 6.28 and a diameter of 4 gives 12.56

decoys.why: This is the area formula, so it gives square units instead of the distance around.
This adds pi instead of multiplying, so the circumference would not grow in step with the diameter.

modeling.title: Planning a round garden bed
modeling.scenario: A fictional school garden club plans a round bed. It needs border stones for the edge and soil for the inside, and each costs a different amount.

given.label: Area covered by one bag of soil

assumptions: The bed is a perfect circle.
Border stones are sold by the meter and can be cut to any length.
Soil bags cannot be split.
prompts: What is the circumference of the bed, and what does the border cost?
What is the area of the bed, and how many bags of soil must the club buy?
If the club doubles the diameter to 16 meters, how many times larger is the area?
limits: Real beds are not perfect circles, so measurements are approximate.
Using 3.14 for pi gives a close estimate, not an exact value.

sentence.base: A circle with a diameter of 10 meters has a circumference of about 31.4 meters.
sentence.because: A circle with a diameter of 10 meters has a circumference of about 31.4 meters because the circumference is pi times the diameter, and 3.14 × 10 = 31.4.
sentence.but: The circumference is about 31.4 meters, but the area is measured in square meters.
sentence.so: The diameter is 10 meters, so the radius is 5 meters and the area is about 78.5 square meters.

diagnostic.prompt: A round pizza has a diameter of 12 inches. Find its circumference and its area using 3.14. Say which answer is a length and which is a square measure.
lookFor: Finds the circumference as 3.14 × 12 = 37.68 inches
Halves the diameter to get the radius 6 and finds the area as 3.14 × 36 = 113.04 square inches
Gives inches for the length and square inches for the area
diagnostic.language: Let the student label a drawing of the pizza with diameter, radius and edge before explaining. If the labels are right, the barrier is the vocabulary, not the formulas.

extension.task: Two angles on a straight line are in the ratio 1 to 5. Find both angle measures, then find the angle across from the smaller one.
extension.reasoning: Explain how you know the two angles are supplementary and not complementary.

en.learning: Your child is learning to find the distance around a circle and the space inside it, and to find missing angles where lines cross.
en.say: The distance around a circle is a little more than 3 times the distance across it.
en.ask: A round table is 4 feet across. About how long is its edge if we use 3 for pi?
en.activity: Find three round objects at home, like a plate and a cup. Wrap string around each one and measure it, then measure across and see how many times it fits around.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a hallar la distancia alrededor de un círculo y el espacio dentro de él, y a hallar ángulos que faltan donde se cruzan líneas.
es.say: La distancia alrededor de un círculo es un poco más de 3 veces la distancia de un lado al otro.
es.ask: Una mesa redonda mide 4 pies de un lado al otro. ¿Cuánto mide su borde, más o menos, si usamos 3 para pi?
es.activity: Busquen tres objetos redondos en casa, como un plato y una taza. Den la vuelta a cada uno con un hilo y midan el hilo, luego midan de un lado al otro y vean cuántas veces cabe alrededor.

skills.objective: Students find probabilities of simple and compound events using sample spaces, compare theoretical and experimental probability, and use probability to predict how often an event will happen.
skills.studentObjective: I can find the probability of an event, list all the outcomes of a compound event, and compare what I expect with what happens.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain a probability using because, but and so with the words sample space, event and experimental probability.
successCriteria: I list a sample space and count the outcomes that belong to the event.
I write a probability as a fraction, a decimal or a percent between 0 and 1.
I find the probability of a compound event by listing outcomes or by multiplying.
I explain why experimental results can differ from theoretical probability.
skills.bigIdea: Probability measures how likely an event is, and what happens in a few trials can differ from what the sample space predicts.

syntax: The probability of ___ is ___ out of ___ because ___.
The experimental result was ___, but the theoretical probability is ___.
discourse: Compare what is expected with what happened
Argue whether a game is fair using numbers

domains.listening: Students listen to a bag of marbles described aloud and name the sample space and a probability.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they listed the outcomes and why they are equally likely.
domains.reading: Students read a carnival game report and underline each probability and the trials it came from.
