vocab.def: A number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely an event is.
vocab.example: 2 out of 5 for landing on an even number on the spinner
vocab.nonExample: 3/2, because a probability cannot be greater than 1
vocab.sentence: The probability of an even number is 2 out of 5.

vocab.def: The list of all possible outcomes of a probability experiment.
vocab.example: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 for the spinner
vocab.nonExample: Only the outcomes you hope for, like 2 and 4
vocab.sentence: The sample space has five outcomes.

visual.caption: All 10 outcomes of a spin and a coin flip

vocab.def: A set of outcomes that you are interested in.
vocab.example: Spinning an even number, which is 2 or 4
vocab.nonExample: The school carnival itself
vocab.sentence: The event even and heads has 2 outcomes.
vocab.everyday: Something that happens, like a school concert

vocab.def: An event with two or more steps, like a spin and then a coin flip.
vocab.example: Spinning a 4 and then flipping heads
vocab.nonExample: Spinning the spinner one time
vocab.sentence: A spin and then a coin flip is a compound event.

vocab.def: Every outcome is equally likely to happen.
vocab.example: A coin that lands on heads or tails with the same chance
vocab.nonExample: A coin that is bent so it lands on heads more often
vocab.sentence: The game uses a fair coin.

vocab.def: The fraction of trials in which an event really happened.
vocab.example: 18 even numbers in 40 spins gives 18/40
vocab.nonExample: 2/5, which comes from counting equally likely outcomes
vocab.sentence: Maya finds the experimental probability of an even number.

misconceptions.belief: After several heads in a row, tails is more likely on the next flip.
misconceptions.why: Students expect results to even out quickly, so they think a fair coin must balance its recent past.
misconceptions.fix: Flip a real coin and record each flip. Ask whether the coin remembers what happened before.

errorCase.story: Cal flips a fair coin and gets heads 4 times in a row.
steps: The coin is fair, so each flip is heads with probability 1/2.
Four heads in a row have happened, so tails is due and has a probability greater than 1/2 next.
The next flip is more likely to be tails.
errorCase.explain: A fair coin has no memory. The next flip is still heads with probability 1/2 and tails with probability 1/2.

misconceptions.belief: When you flip two coins, the number of heads (0, 1, 2) lists the outcomes, so each is equally likely.
misconceptions.why: Students list the results they see at the end and skip the order of the coins.
misconceptions.fix: Name the coins, such as a penny and a nickel, and list pairs: penny first, then nickel. Count the pairs.

errorCase.story: Two fair coins are flipped, and the question asks for the probability of two heads.
steps: Flip two fair coins and count the heads: 0, 1 or 2.
That is 3 outcomes, so the chance of 2 heads is 1/3.
errorCase.explain: The outcomes 0, 1 and 2 heads are not equally likely. The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT, so the chance of two heads is 1/4.

misconceptions.belief: A fair game always gives results that match the probabilities after only a few trials.
misconceptions.why: The word fair sounds like it means even, so students expect an even split every time.
misconceptions.fix: Use fair to describe the chances of each outcome, not the results in a few trials. Compare 10 spins with 100 spins.

misconceptions.belief: To find the probability of A and then B, add the two probabilities.
misconceptions.why: Students link the word and with adding, and do not picture the smaller part of the sample space where both happen.
misconceptions.fix: Draw a tree diagram or list all outcomes of both steps and count only the ones where both events happen.

reading.title: The Carnival Spinner
reading.text: At the school carnival, a game uses a spinner with 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5, and a fair coin. The probability of landing on an even number is 2 out of 5, because the sample space has five outcomes and two of them, 2 and 4, are even. In a compound event, a player spins and then flips the coin. The sample space now has 10 outcomes, and the event even and heads has 2 of them, so its probability is 2 out of 10, or 1/5. Maya tests the game 40 times and spins an even number 18 times. Her experimental probability is 18/40, which is 0.45, a bit more than the theoretical 0.4. She says the spinner must be unfair, but a small difference is normal when the number of trials is small.
reading.simple: A carnival game uses a spinner with 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5, and a fair coin. The probability of an even number is 2 out of 5, because 2 and 4 are even. A player spins and then flips the coin. There are 10 outcomes, and even and heads is 2 of them, so the probability is 1/5. Maya tests the game 40 times and gets an even number 18 times. Her experimental probability is 18/40, which is 0.45. The theoretical probability is 0.4.

questions.q: How many outcomes are in the sample space for a spin and a coin flip?
questions.a: 10 outcomes

questions.q: Why does Maya's experimental result differ from the theoretical probability even though the game is fair?
questions.a: She tried the game only 40 times. Small numbers of trials often differ a little from what theory predicts.

questions.q: How do you know the probability of even and heads is 1/5?
questions.a: Two of the 10 equally likely outcomes, 2H and 4H, are even and heads, and 2 out of 10 is 1/5.

wdntb.why: 1/3 is about 33%, a different probability. The other three all show a probability of one fourth.

noticeWonder.prompt: Maya spun the spinner 40 times and got an even number 18 times. The spinner has 2 even sections out of 5. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A probability can never be greater than 1.
asn.why: An event cannot happen in more outcomes than the sample space holds, so the fraction is at most 1.

asn.claim: If you flip a fair coin 10 times, you will get exactly 5 heads.
asn.why: 5 heads is the most likely single result, but 4 or 6 heads are common too.

wyr.q: Would you rather find all outcomes of two steps with a table or with a tree diagram?

compare.a: Una lists HH, HT, TH and TT for two coins and counts 1 outcome with two heads out of 4.
compare.prompt: Do both strategies give the same probability? Why does multiplying work?

debate.claim: A fair coin that lands on heads 6 times in a row must be unfair.
debate.forEvidence: Six heads in a row feels too unlikely to happen by chance.
debate.againstEvidence: For a fair coin, 6 heads in a row has probability 1/64, which is small but happens about once in every 64 tries.

listening.script: Listen to Jamal describe a bag of marbles. The bag holds 4 green marbles, 3 blue marbles, and 5 red marbles, all the same size. I will draw one marble without looking. The total is 12 marbles, so the probability of blue is 3 out of 12, which is one fourth. Now I put the marble back and draw again. Drawing blue twice is a compound event. I multiply one fourth times one fourth and get 1 out of 16. My sister adds one fourth and one fourth and says one half. But one half is much too big for getting two blue marbles in a row.

tasks.q: What is the probability of drawing a blue marble on one draw?
tasks.why: There are 3 blue marbles among 12, and 3 out of 12 is 1 out of 4.

tasks.q: Why can the probability of two blue marbles in a row not be one half?
options: Two blue draws in a row is less likely than one blue draw, so it must be less than one fourth.
There are only 12 marbles in the bag.
Two draws always give a probability of one half.
tasks.why: Both draws must be blue, so the probability is smaller than the chance of one blue draw: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

story.title: The Fair Prize Game
story.goal: design a prize game that is fair and still raises money
story.intro: Soren builds a prize game for the school fair. Players spin a wheel, and Soren wants every player to have a real chance while the class still raises money for a field trip.

beats.lead: Soren draws the wheel and lists every possible outcome.
beats.success: The sample space is complete, and each outcome is equally likely.
beats.redirect: Some outcomes seem bigger than others, so Soren redraws the sections to make them equal.

beats.lead: Soren finds the probability of a prize and predicts how many winners to expect.
beats.success: He multiplies the probability by the number of players and gets a clear prediction.
beats.redirect: The prediction looks too high, so Soren checks how many sections are prizes.

beats.lead: After the first hour, the number of winners is a little different from the prediction.
beats.success: Soren explains that small samples vary, and he waits for more players before changing the wheel.
beats.redirect: Soren worries the wheel is broken, so he compares the results with the expected number and the number of trials.

story.ending: The game stays fair, the class earns money, and Soren can explain why results vary.

panels.says: I rolled a fair number cube 6 times and got a 6 three times!
That is a high experimental result, but the theoretical probability of a 6 is 1 out of 6.
So the cube must be unfair?
Not yet. Roll it 60 more times and see if the results move closer to 1 out of 6.

predict.q: Dani rolls the cube 60 more times. Before Priya answers, predict the number of 6s that theory expects.
predict.why: The probability of a 6 is 1/6, and 1/6 of 60 is 10.

transfer.relationship: The probability is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the number of equally likely outcomes in the sample space
phrasings: 2 of the 5 equally likely outcomes are even
P(even) = 2/5
About 4 out of every 10 spins should be even in the long run
A 40% chance of spinning an even number

decoys.why: This compares 2 even outcomes with 3 odd outcomes, not with all 5 outcomes.
Even and odd are not equally likely on this spinner, because only 2 of the 5 sections are even.

modeling.scenario: A fictional class runs a spinner game at a school fair. Players pay a ticket price and win a small prize when the spinner lands on a prize section.
assumptions: Every section of the spinner is equally likely.
Each player spins exactly once.
Each player pays the ticket price.
prompts: What is the probability that a player wins a prize?
About how many winners should the class expect among 50 players, and what will the prizes cost?
At one booth, 19 of 50 players win. Does that prove the spinner is unfair? Explain.

A real spinner can be slightly uneven, which this model ignores.

sentence.base: The probability of an even number on the spinner is 2 out of 5.
sentence.because: The probability of an even number on the spinner is 2 out of 5 because two of the five equally likely outcomes, 2 and 4, are even.
sentence.but: Maya's experimental result was a little higher, but the theoretical probability is still 2 out of 5.
sentence.so: The sample space has five equally likely outcomes, so each outcome has a probability of 1 out of 5.

diagnostic.prompt: A bag has 3 red cubes and 5 blue cubes. Find the probability of drawing red. Then you draw a cube, put it back and draw again. Find the probability of drawing red both times.
lookFor: Finds the probability of red as 3 out of 8
Lists or multiplies to find 3/8 × 3/8 = 9/64
Explains that the second draw has the same chances because the cube was put back

extension.task: Design a spinner with three colors where blue has probability 1/2, and red is twice as likely as green. Give each probability.
extension.reasoning: Explain why the three probabilities must add up to 1.

en.learning: Your child is learning how to measure chance, like the chance of picking a red sock from a drawer, and to list all the possible results.
en.say: A probability tells how many of the possible results are the ones we want, out of all of them.
en.ask: A bag has 2 red socks and 3 blue socks. If you pick without looking, what is the chance of red?
en.activity: Flip a coin 20 times and keep a tally. Ask your child how many heads you expect, and what they notice when the results are a little different.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a medir la posibilidad, como la posibilidad de sacar un calcetín rojo de un cajón, y a hacer una lista de todos los resultados posibles.
es.say: Una probabilidad dice cuántos de los resultados posibles son los que queremos, de entre todos.
es.ask: Una bolsa tiene 2 calcetines rojos y 3 calcetines azules. Si sacan uno sin mirar, ¿cuál es la probabilidad de que sea rojo?

skills.objective: Students distinguish a population from a sample, judge whether a sampling method is random and representative, and use the proportions in a random sample to make and justify inferences about a population.
skills.studentObjective: I can tell whether a sample is fair, and I can use a random sample to estimate something about a whole population.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain why a sample is or is not fair and what it tells us using because, but and so with the words population, random sample and inference.
successCriteria: I name the population and the sample in a survey.
I say whether a sampling method is random and give a reason.
I use the percent in a sample to estimate a number for the whole population.
I explain why two random samples can give different estimates.
skills.bigIdea: A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance, so its results can support a careful estimate about the whole group.

syntax: The sample is biased because ___.
The sample suggests that about ___% of the population ___, so I estimate ___.
discourse: Critique a survey method and suggest a fairer one
Explain an estimate and why it can be a little off

domains.listening: Students listen to a pet survey plan and decide which sample is fair.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they would choose a sample and why it is fair.
domains.reading: Students read a lunch survey report and mark the population, the sample and the inference.

vocab.def: The whole group you want to learn about.
vocab.example: All 600 students at the school
vocab.nonExample: The 40 students whose names were drawn, which is a sample
vocab.sentence: The whole group of students is the population.

vocab.def: A smaller part of a population that is studied to learn about the whole group.
vocab.example: 40 students chosen from the school
vocab.nonExample: A free taste of juice at a store
vocab.sentence: Diego picks a sample because asking everyone takes too long.
vocab.everyday: A small piece of something you can try, like a free taste at a store

visual.title: Lunch choices in a sample of 40

vocab.def: A sample chosen so that every member of the population has an equal chance of being picked.
vocab.example: Drawing 40 names from a hat that holds every student's name
vocab.nonExample: Asking the first 20 students you meet in the gym
vocab.sentence: The council draws a random sample from a hat.

vocab.def: A way that a sample or a question favors some answers over others.
vocab.example: Surveying only soccer players about favorite sports
vocab.nonExample: Choosing names at random from the whole school
vocab.sentence: Asking only players in the gym leads to bias.
vocab.everyday: An unfair preference for or against someone or something

vocab.def: Describing a sample that shows the same mix as the whole population.
vocab.example: A random sample that includes students from every grade
vocab.nonExample: A sample that includes only one grade
vocab.sentence: A good sample is representative of the population.

vocab.def: A conclusion about a population based on evidence from a sample.
vocab.example: About 45% of all students would pick tacos
vocab.nonExample: Exactly 18 students in the sample picked tacos
vocab.sentence: The council makes an inference from the random sample.
vocab.morphology: in- means into; ferre means to carry

misconceptions.belief: A large sample is always a good sample, even if it was chosen in a biased way.
misconceptions.why: Students link more data with better data and overlook who is left out of the sample.
misconceptions.fix: Compare two surveys of the same size, one random and one from a single group, and ask who each survey leaves out.

errorCase.story: Lena wants to know the favorite hobby of all 600 students in her school.
steps: Lena wants to know the favorite hobby of all 600 students.
She surveys 150 students, all of them from the band room.
The sample is large, so it must represent all 600 students.
errorCase.explain: A large sample from one group still leaves most students out. Choosing members at random matters more than the size of the sample.

misconceptions.belief: The number of students in the sample who gave an answer is the number in the whole population.
misconceptions.why: Students stop at the count they found and forget to scale from the sample to the whole group.
misconceptions.fix: Write the sample as a fraction or percent first. Then ask: if the population is bigger, what number keeps the same part?

errorCase.story: In a random sample of 40 students, 18 chose tacos. The school has 600 students.
steps: In the sample, 18 of 40 students chose tacos.
So the population has 18 taco fans.
The number is 18 out of 600.
errorCase.explain: The sample shows the part, 18 out of 40, which is 45%. For 600 students, 45% of 600 is 270 students.

misconceptions.belief: If two random samples give different results, one of them must be wrong.
misconceptions.why: Students expect a sample to equal the population exactly, so any difference looks like a mistake.
misconceptions.fix: Draw several small samples from a bag of known colors. Record each percent and see how they spread around the true value.

misconceptions.belief: A random sample means picking whoever is easiest to reach.
misconceptions.why: In everyday speech random can mean without a plan, so students think any quick choice counts.
misconceptions.fix: Say that random means every member has an equal chance, and show a list, a hat or a number generator that does it.

reading.title: What Lunch Do We Like?
reading.text: The student council wants to know which lunch the 600 students at Riverside Middle School like best. The whole group is the population. Asking everyone takes too long, so Diego picks a sample. First he asks 20 students in the gym after soccer practice, but those students may not be representative, and the results show bias. Then the council draws 40 names from a hat that holds every student, which makes a random sample. In that sample, 18 students pick tacos. Since 18 out of 40 is 45%, the council makes an inference: about 45% of all 600 students, or 270 students, would pick tacos. The inference is an estimate, so another random sample of 40 students could give a different result.
reading.simple: The student council asks which lunch the 600 students like best. The whole group is the population. Diego asks 20 students after soccer practice, but they may not be representative, so there is bias. The council then draws 40 names from a hat of every student. That is a random sample. In the sample, 18 students pick tacos, and 18 out of 40 is 45%. The council makes an inference: about 45% of all 600 students, or 270 students, would pick tacos. Another random sample might give a different result.

questions.q: How many names does the council draw from the hat?
questions.a: 40 names

questions.q: Why are the 20 students in the gym a poor sample?
questions.a: They are soccer players, so they may not be like the whole school, and not every student had a chance to be asked.

questions.q: How does the council get 270 students from the sample?
questions.a: In the sample 18 out of 40 is 45%, and 45% of 600 is 270.

items: 40 names from a random number list
40 students from a randomly ordered class roster
wdntb.why: The first three give every student an equal chance to be chosen. Players from the gym include only one group, so the sample is biased.

noticeWonder.prompt: In one random sample of 40 students, 18 picked tacos. In another random sample of 40 students, 14 picked tacos. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: Making a biased sample larger fixes the bias.
asn.why: A larger sample from the same biased method still leaves out the same people, so the bias stays.

asn.claim: A random sample is representative of the population.
asn.why: Random sampling usually gives a representative sample, but by chance one sample can miss a group, especially when it is small.

wyr.q: Would you rather estimate with a small random sample or with a large sample of volunteers?

compare.a: Pilar draws 40 names from a hat that holds all 600 student names.
compare.b: Jon asks the first 40 students who walk into the cafeteria.
compare.prompt: Which method is more likely to give a representative sample? What could go wrong with the other?

debate.claim: A sample of 40 students can tell us about all 600 students.
debate.forEvidence: A random sample of 40 has about the same mix as the school: 18 out of 40 is 45%.
debate.againstEvidence: Forty is a small part of 600, so another sample could give a different percent.

listening.script: Listen to Keisha explain her pet survey. Our town has 2,000 households. I want to estimate how many own a dog. I get a list of all households and use a random number generator to pick 50. In my sample, 20 households own a dog. That is 20 out of 50, or 40%. So I estimate that about 40% of the 2,000 households, or 800 households, own a dog. My friend asked 50 people outside a dog park. Her sample would give a much higher number, because people at a dog park are more likely to own dogs.

tasks.q: About how many households does Keisha estimate own a dog?
tasks.why: 20 out of 50 is 40%, and 40% of 2,000 is 800.

tasks.q: Why would the sample from the dog park give a poor estimate?
options: People at a dog park are more likely to own a dog, so the sample is biased.
Fifty people is too few to ask.
Dogs cannot be counted at a park.
tasks.why: The dog park sample leaves out people who do not own dogs, so it does not represent the town.

story.title: What Should the Park Add?
story.goal: find out what the park should add next
story.intro: Nia helps the neighborhood association decide what to add to the park. She cannot ask every neighbor, so she must choose a sample that speaks for everyone.

beats.lead: Nia thinks about how to choose neighbors to ask.
beats.success: She picks names at random from the full list, so every neighbor has a chance.
beats.redirect: Her list only has neighbors near the park, so Nia adds the missing streets.

beats.lead: The first sample shows a clear favorite idea for the park.
beats.success: Nia finds the percent in the sample and uses it to estimate for all neighbors.
beats.redirect: Her estimate looks too small, so Nia checks that she scaled up from the sample.

beats.lead: A second sample gives a slightly different percent.
beats.success: Nia explains that samples vary and combines the two to get a steadier estimate.
beats.redirect: Nia worries one sample was wrong, so she compares both with the size of each sample.

story.ending: The association picks a new feature for the park, and Nia can explain how the sample supports the choice.

panels.says: I will ask my first 10 friends which school club is best.
Your friends are not the whole school. That is a biased sample.
Okay, so how do I choose fairly?
Give every student a number and pick 30 numbers at random.

predict.q: Omar's random sample of 30 students shows that 12 like robotics. Before Leila answers, predict about what percent of the whole school likes robotics.
predict.why: 12 out of 30 is 40%, so about 40% of the whole school may like robotics.

transfer.relationship: The part of a random sample that has a feature estimates the part of the population that has it
phrasings: 18 out of 40 sampled students picked tacos, so about 45% of the school would
The sample proportion of 0.45 estimates the population proportion
From 18 of 40 students, about 270 of 600 students
Since 40 × 15 = 600, multiply 18 by 15 to estimate 270

decoys.why: This uses the count from the sample as if it were the count for the whole population.

decoys.why: The sample is large, but it is not random, so it may not represent the whole school.

modeling.scenario: A fictional neighborhood has 800 residents. A group draws two random samples of 60 residents each and asks whether they want a new playground.

given.label: Yes answers in the first sample
Yes answers in the second sample

assumptions: Each sample was chosen at random from a full list of residents.
Everyone answered honestly.
No resident was in both samples.
prompts: Use the first sample to estimate how many of the 800 residents want a playground.
Use the second sample the same way. Why do the two estimates differ?
Combine both samples to get one estimate. Why might it be more reliable?
limits: A sample estimate is not the exact number, so the true answer could be a little different.
Residents might change their minds after the survey.

sentence.base: A random sample can help us estimate what a whole population thinks.
sentence.because: A random sample can help us estimate what a whole population thinks because every member of the population has an equal chance of being picked.
sentence.but: A random sample is much smaller than the population, but it can still give a useful estimate.
sentence.so: The sample was random, so the council can use 18 out of 40 to estimate about 270 of 600 students.

diagnostic.prompt: A school has 500 students. A random sample of 50 students shows that 15 walk to school. Estimate how many of all students walk, and explain why the sample can be trusted.
lookFor: Finds 15 out of 50 is 30%
Finds 30% of 500 is about 150 students
Says the sample was random, so every student had a chance to be picked

skills.objective: Students compare proportional relationships shown as tables, graphs, equations and verbal descriptions by finding each unit rate and decide which relationship has the greater rate or the lower cost.

skills.languageObjective: I will explain how two representations show the same relationship using because, but and so with the words representation, unit rate and ordered pair.
successCriteria: I find the unit rate from a table, a graph, an equation and a description.
I compare two relationships by comparing their unit rates, not their totals.
I match a table, a graph and an equation that describe the same relationship.
I explain which representation helps most for a given question.
skills.bigIdea: A table, a graph, an equation and a description can all show the same relationship, and the unit rate is what lets us compare them.

syntax: In the table, the unit rate is ___ because ___ divided by ___ is ___.
The graph and the equation show the same relationship because both have the unit rate ___.
discourse: Compare two representations and justify which one is greater
Describe where to find the unit rate in each representation

vocab.def: A way of showing a mathematical idea, such as a table, graph, equation or words.
vocab.example: A graph of distance and time
vocab.nonExample: A guess with no work shown
vocab.sentence: Each student uses a different representation.
vocab.morphology: re- means again; present means to show, so to show again

vocab.def: Rows and columns that list pairs of values side by side.
vocab.example: A table of seconds and meters for a model car
vocab.nonExample: A table where you eat lunch
vocab.sentence: Sam makes a table of his car's distances.
vocab.everyday: A piece of furniture with a flat top and legs

vocab.def: A picture that shows pairs of values as points on a coordinate plane.
vocab.example: A straight line through the corner where the axes start and the point (5, 20)
vocab.nonExample: A list of numbers with no axes
vocab.sentence: Uma draws a graph of her car's distance and time.

vocab.def: A statement with an equal sign, like d = 3t, that links two quantities.
vocab.example: d = 3t
vocab.nonExample: The expression 3t, which has no equal sign
vocab.sentence: Tia writes an equation for her car.

vocab.def: The amount of one quantity for exactly 1 of the other quantity.
vocab.example: 3.5 meters per second
vocab.nonExample: 7 meters in 2 seconds, which is not yet for 1 second
vocab.sentence: The unit rate lets us compare two cars.

vocab.def: Two numbers (x, y) that name one point on a graph.
vocab.nonExample: The sum 5 + 20
vocab.sentence: The ordered pair (5, 20) is a point on Uma's graph.

misconceptions.belief: To compare two relationships, compare any two outputs you can find.
misconceptions.why: Students compare the numbers they see first, even when those numbers belong to different inputs.
misconceptions.fix: Always compare at the same input, or compare unit rates. Ask: for how many of the first quantity is each output?

errorCase.story: Plan A is a table showing that 4 tickets cost 10 dollars. Plan B is the equation y = 2x, where x is the number of tickets.
steps: Plan A: 4 tickets cost 10 dollars, and Plan B is y = 2x, where x is tickets.
Plan B for 6 tickets costs 2 × 6 = 12 dollars.
12 is more than 10, so Plan B costs more per ticket.
errorCase.explain: The two costs are for different numbers of tickets. Per ticket, Plan A costs 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 dollars and Plan B costs 2 dollars, so Plan A costs more per ticket.

misconceptions.belief: The unit rate is the y-value of the last point on a graph.
misconceptions.why: Students read the largest y-value because it is easy to see, and forget that a unit rate is for exactly 1 of the first quantity.
misconceptions.fix: Find the point where x is 1, or divide y by x for any point. Mark that point on the line.

errorCase.story: A graph shows a straight line through (0, 0) and (5, 20) for distance and time.
steps: The graph is a straight line through (0, 0) and (5, 20).
The unit rate is the y-value at the end of the line, which is 20.
So the car goes 20 meters per second.
errorCase.explain: The unit rate is the y-value when x is 1. Divide: 20 ÷ 5 = 4, so the point (1, 4) is on the line and the car goes 4 meters per second.

misconceptions.belief: A table where y goes up by the same amount each time shows a proportional relationship.
misconceptions.why: Students notice a steady pattern and treat any steady pattern as proportional.
misconceptions.fix: Add a column for y divided by x. A proportional table has the same value in every row, and the pair x = 0, y = 0 would fit.

misconceptions.belief: Meters per second and seconds per meter mean the same thing.
misconceptions.why: The word per is read as a link between the two quantities without noticing which one is compared to 1.
misconceptions.fix: Say each rate in words with a number: 3.5 meters per second means 3.5 meters for 1 second. Then say the reverse and compare.

reading.title: Three Cars, Three Representations
reading.text: Three students compare how fast their model cars travel. Each student uses a different representation. Sam shares a table: after 2 seconds his car is 7 meters from the start, and after 4 seconds it is 14 meters. Tia shares the equation d = 3t, where d is meters and t is seconds. Uma draws a graph with a straight line through the ordered pair (5, 20) and the corner where both axes start. All three show proportional relationships, but the unit rate is hidden in a different place each time. In Sam's table, 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5 meters per second. In Tia's equation, the number multiplying t is 3. On Uma's graph, 20 ÷ 5 = 4. So Uma's car is the fastest and Tia's car is the slowest.
reading.simple: Three students compare how fast their model cars travel. Sam makes a table: after 2 seconds his car is 7 meters from the start, and after 4 seconds it is 14 meters. Tia writes the equation d = 3t. Uma draws a graph through the ordered pair (5, 20). Each representation shows a unit rate. For Sam, 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5 meters per second. For Tia, the unit rate is 3. For Uma, 20 ÷ 5 = 4. So Uma's car is the fastest and Tia's car is the slowest.

questions.q: How far is Sam's car from the start after 4 seconds?
questions.a: 14 meters

questions.q: Where is the unit rate in Tia's equation, and what does it mean?
questions.a: It is the number multiplying t, 3, so her car moves 3 meters each second.

questions.q: Which car is the fastest, and how do you know?
questions.a: Uma's car, because 4 meters per second is greater than 3.5 and 3.

wdntb.why: y = x + 3 adds 3 instead of multiplying. The other three show y = 3x in different representations.

noticeWonder.prompt: A table shows 2 seconds and 7 meters, then 4 seconds and 14 meters. An equation says d = 3t. A graph passes through (5, 20). What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If a table, a graph and an equation describe the same proportional relationship, they have the same unit rate.
asn.why: The unit rate is a property of the relationship, so every representation of it must show the same number.

asn.claim: The graph that looks steepest always has the greatest unit rate.
asn.why: If two graphs use different scales on the axes, one can look steeper even when its unit rate is smaller.

wyr.q: Would you rather compare two relationships with tables or with graphs?

compare.a: Lia divides y by x in the table and at a point of the graph, then compares 3.5 and 4.
compare.b: Max draws both relationships on the same axes and sees which line is higher at x = 5.
compare.prompt: Do both strategies show which car is faster? When is each one more useful?

debate.claim: A graph shows a unit rate more clearly than an equation does.
debate.forEvidence: On a graph you can see the steepness of the line at a glance.
debate.againstEvidence: In d = 3t the unit rate is the number 3, with nothing to read or estimate.

listening.script: Listen to Cleo compare two phone plans. Plan one is a table. It says 3 gigabytes cost 12 dollars, and 5 gigabytes cost 20 dollars. Plan two is an equation. The cost c equals 3.5 times g, where g is the number of gigabytes. For plan one, 12 divided by 3 is 4 dollars per gigabyte, and 20 divided by 5 is also 4. For plan two, the unit rate is 3.5. One plan is a table and the other is an equation, but I can still compare the unit rates. Plan two costs less per gigabyte.

tasks.q: Which plan costs less per gigabyte?
tasks.why: Plan two costs 3.5 dollars per gigabyte, and plan one costs 4 dollars per gigabyte.

tasks.q: In plan two's equation, which part is the unit rate?
tasks.why: The number multiplying g is the cost for 1 gigabyte, so 3.5 is the unit rate.

story.title: One Relationship, Three Displays
story.goal: show that a table, a graph and an equation can describe one relationship
story.intro: Selma tests how quickly a water filter cleans water. Visitors at the science fair look at different displays, and she wants every display to tell the same story.

beats.lead: Selma records her measurements in a table at the start of the fair.
beats.success: She finds the same unit rate in every row and writes it at the top of the table.
beats.redirect: The rates do not match, so Selma checks which quantity she divided by which.

beats.lead: She turns the table into an equation and a graph for her poster.
beats.success: The equation and the graph both show her unit rate, and the three displays agree.
beats.redirect: The graph disagrees with the table, so Selma checks where her line crosses the axes.

beats.lead: A visitor asks how her filter compares with a second filter shown as an equation.
beats.success: Selma compares the two unit rates and explains which filter is faster.
beats.redirect: She is not sure which is faster, so she finds both rates in the same units.

story.ending: The poster shows one relationship in three ways, and Selma can explain how to read the unit rate in each one.

panels.says: My table says 2 hours of tutoring cost 30 dollars, and 3 hours cost 45 dollars.
Mine is the equation y = 14x, where x is hours.
To compare, I find my unit rate: 30 ÷ 2 = 15 dollars per hour.
Mine is 14 dollars per hour, so my tutor charges less per hour.

predict.q: Mira graphs her equation. Before Jae answers, predict the point on her graph where x is 3.
predict.why: For y = 14x, 14 × 3 = 42, so the point is (3, 42).

transfer.relationship: The second quantity is always 4 times the first, so the unit rate is 4
phrasings: A car moves 4 meters each second
d = 4t
A table with the pairs (1, 4), (2, 8) and (5, 20)
A graph: a straight line through the corner where the axes start and the point (5, 20)

decoys.why: This adds 4 instead of multiplying, so the distance is not 4 times the time.

decoys.text: A table with the pairs (1, 5), (2, 6) and (5, 9)
decoys.why: Each y is 4 more than x, which is adding, not multiplying.

modeling.title: Comparing two water filters
modeling.scenario: A fictional science club tests two water filters. Filter A is described by a table, and Filter B is described by an equation.
assumptions: Each filter cleans water at a steady rate.
Both filters start with no water cleaned.
The water is the same dirtiness for both filters.
prompts: Find the unit rate of Filter A and of Filter B. Which filter is faster?
Write an equation for Filter A.
How many minutes does each filter need to clean 27 liters?
limits: Real filters slow down as they clog, so the steady rate is only an approximation.
Two tests are not many, so the rate of Filter A is an estimate.

sentence.base: A table, a graph and an equation can show one proportional relationship.
sentence.because: A table, a graph and an equation can show one proportional relationship because each one can show the same unit rate.
sentence.but: A table and an equation look very different, but they can describe the same relationship.
sentence.so: Sam's table shows 3.5 meters each second, so Uma's car, at 4 meters each second, is faster.

diagnostic.prompt: Shop A has a table showing 3 notebooks for 6 dollars and 5 notebooks for 10 dollars. Shop B uses the equation y = 2.5x, where x is notebooks. Which shop charges less per notebook? Show how you compare.
lookFor: Finds Shop A's unit rate as 2 dollars per notebook
Reads Shop B's unit rate as 2.5 from the equation
Compares the unit rates and says Shop A charges less
diagnostic.language: Let the student point to where each rate is found before explaining. If the rates are correct, the barrier is the language of comparison, not the proportional reasoning.

extension.task: Make up a proportional relationship with a unit rate of 2.4. Show it as a table, an equation and a description of the graph, and check that all three agree.
extension.reasoning: Explain which representation makes the unit rate easiest to see and which one makes a prediction easiest.

en.learning: Your child is learning to compare prices or speeds that are shown in different ways, like a table, an equation or a graph.
en.say: To compare, find the amount for exactly 1 in each one, like the price for 1 apple.
en.ask: Store A says 3 apples cost 6 dollars. Store B says the cost is 1.5 times the number of apples. Which store is cheaper per apple?
en.activity: Look at two store flyers together. Ask your child to find the price for 1 of the same item in each flyer and say which is the better deal.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a comparar precios o velocidades que se muestran de maneras distintas, como una tabla, una ecuación o una gráfica.
es.say: Para comparar, hallen la cantidad para exactamente 1 en cada uno, como el precio de 1 manzana.
es.ask: La tienda A dice que 3 manzanas cuestan 6 dólares. La tienda B dice que el costo es 1.5 veces el número de manzanas. ¿Qué tienda es más barata por manzana?

skills.objective: Students construct and critique mathematical arguments about proportional relationships by stating a claim, giving evidence from tables, graphs and equations, and using counterexamples to test whether a claim is always true.
skills.studentObjective: I can make a claim about a proportional relationship, support it with evidence, and use a counterexample to test a claim.
skills.languageObjective: I will build an argument using because, but and so with the words claim, evidence and counterexample.
successCriteria: I state a clear claim before I give my reasons.
I support a claim with evidence from a table, a graph or an equation.
I find a counterexample when a claim is not always true.
I explain why a reason that works for every case is stronger than one example.
skills.bigIdea: An argument in mathematics needs a claim and evidence that works for every case, and one counterexample is enough to show a claim is not always true.

syntax: My claim is ___. My evidence is ___, so ___.
This is a counterexample because ___ does not work when ___.
discourse: Support a claim with evidence and a reason
Respond to a partner's claim with agreement, a question or a counterexample

domains.speaking: Students present a claim to a partner and respond to the partner's counterexample.

vocab.def: A statement that you say is true and then try to support.
vocab.example: The total cost is proportional to the number of shirts
vocab.nonExample: A question like how many shirts did we buy
vocab.sentence: Amara makes a claim about the cost of shirts.
vocab.everyday: To say that something belongs to you, like claiming a lost coat

vocab.def: Facts, numbers or examples that show a claim is true.
vocab.example: A table showing 6 dollars for every shirt, both times
vocab.nonExample: I just feel that it is true
vocab.sentence: Luca asks Amara for evidence.

vocab.def: One example that shows a claim is not always true.
vocab.example: A shop with a 25 dollar setup fee, where the ratios are 8.5 and 7.25
vocab.nonExample: Another example where the claim works
vocab.sentence: Luca finds a counterexample to Amara's claim.
vocab.morphology: counter- means against, so an example against a claim

vocab.def: To give clear reasons that show why a claim is true.
vocab.example: Showing that dividing the first quantity by the second always gives the same number
vocab.nonExample: Saying it is true because I said so
vocab.sentence: To justify a claim, give reasons that work for every case.
vocab.morphology: just means fair or right; -ify means to make

vocab.def: Correct in its reasoning, so the evidence supports the conclusion.
vocab.example: An argument that uses the same ratio in every case
vocab.nonExample: An argument based on one lucky example
vocab.sentence: Marcus agrees that the argument is valid.
vocab.everyday: Allowed or accepted, like a valid bus ticket

misconceptions.belief: If a claim works in one example, it is true for every case.
misconceptions.why: Students are used to checking an answer, and a single successful check feels like proof.
misconceptions.fix: Ask what would have to be true for every case. Test the claim with a very different example and look for one that fails.

errorCase.story: Bo claims that adding the same number to both parts of a ratio keeps the ratio equivalent.
steps: Bo's claim: adding the same number to both parts of a ratio keeps the ratio equivalent.
Test: 1 to 1, add 3 to each, gives 4 to 4, and 4 to 4 is equivalent to 1 to 1.
One example works, so the claim is always true.
errorCase.explain: One example cannot prove a claim for every case. Try 1 to 2: adding 3 gives 4 to 5, but an equivalent ratio would be 4 to 8. That counterexample shows the claim is false.

misconceptions.belief: Saying the claim again with the word because is evidence.
misconceptions.why: The word because makes a sentence sound like a reason even when it only repeats what was claimed.
misconceptions.fix: Ask what numbers or steps show it. Evidence names something you can check, like a multiplication, a table or a graph.

errorCase.story: Pia claims that 9 cups of flour to 6 cups of sugar tastes the same as 3 cups of flour to 2 cups of sugar.
steps: Claim: 3 to 2 is equivalent to 9 to 6.
Evidence: they are equivalent because they are the same recipe.
So the claim is true.
errorCase.explain: That evidence only repeats the claim. Real evidence uses the mathematics: 3 × 3 = 9 and 2 × 3 = 6, so both parts were multiplied by the same number.

misconceptions.belief: A graph that is a straight line is enough evidence that a relationship is proportional.
misconceptions.why: Students remember the straight line and forget the second condition: the line must pass through the origin.
misconceptions.fix: Ask for a second piece of evidence, such as the point for 0 or the ratio y divided by x in two rows.

misconceptions.belief: A claim that something is always true is fine if it is true most of the time.
misconceptions.why: In everyday talk always is often used loosely, but in mathematics it means every case without exception.
misconceptions.fix: Say always means every single case. Practice finding the one case that breaks a claim.

reading.title: Amara's Claim About Shirts
reading.text: Amara makes a claim: if a print shop charges the same price for every T-shirt, then the total cost is always proportional to the number of shirts. Her partner Luca asks for evidence. Amara shows a table: 10 shirts cost 60 dollars and 20 shirts cost 120 dollars, so the cost for each shirt is 6 dollars both times. Luca tests a different shop. It charges a setup fee of 25 dollars plus 6 dollars per shirt. For 10 shirts the cost is 85 dollars, and for 20 shirts it is 145 dollars. The ratios 8.5 and 7.25 are not equal, so this shop's cost is not proportional. Luca's example is a counterexample to Amara's claim. To justify a claim, you need reasons that work for every case, not only for one example. Amara changes her claim: if there is no setup fee, the total cost is proportional.
reading.simple: Amara makes a claim: if a print shop charges the same price for every T-shirt, the total cost is proportional to the number of shirts. Luca asks for evidence. Amara shows that 10 shirts cost 60 dollars and 20 shirts cost 120 dollars, which is 6 dollars each time. Luca tests another shop with a setup fee of 25 dollars plus 6 dollars per shirt. It costs 85 dollars for 10 shirts and 145 dollars for 20 shirts. The ratios 8.5 and 7.25 are not equal. This is a counterexample.

questions.q: What does the second print shop charge for 20 shirts?
questions.a: 145 dollars

questions.q: Why does Amara change her claim?
questions.a: Luca's counterexample shows that a shop with a setup fee has a cost that is not proportional, so the claim was not always true.

questions.q: How do you know that the second shop's cost is not proportional?
questions.a: 85 ÷ 10 = 8.5 and 145 ÷ 20 = 7.25, so the cost per shirt is not constant.

wdntb.why: The first three each have a unit rate of 6. 20 for 5 has a unit rate of 4, so it is not equivalent to the others.

asn.claim: One counterexample is enough to show that a claim is not always true.
asn.why: A claim about every case fails as soon as there is a single case where it does not work.

asn.claim: If a relationship works for the first three pairs in a table, it works for every pair.
asn.why: It may, but a pattern can change later, so you need a reason that covers every case.

wyr.q: Would you rather justify a claim with a table of examples or with a reason that works for every case?
wyr.b: A reason that works for every case

compare.a: Kira tests three pairs of ratios and finds the same unit rate in each.
compare.b: Kira explains that dividing the first quantity by the second gives the unit rate, which must be the same in both ratios, so it works for any pair.
compare.prompt: Which argument is stronger? What does the second add that the first does not?

debate.claim: A claim that works for three examples is proven.
debate.forEvidence: Three examples is a lot, and all three of them worked.
debate.againstEvidence: A claim has to work for every case, and one counterexample, like a shop with a 25 dollar setup fee, can break it.

listening.script: Listen to a debate in Mr. Ortiz's class. Kira says, I claim that if two ratios have the same unit rate, they are equivalent. Here is my evidence. Twelve miles in 3 hours is 4 miles per hour, and 20 miles in 5 hours is also 4 miles per hour, and the ratios 12 to 3 and 20 to 5 are equivalent. Marcus says, you have shown only one case. So Kira adds a reason: dividing the first quantity by the second gives the same number, so both ratios equal 4 to 1. Marcus agrees that this reason works for every pair of ratios, not just one.

tasks.q: What unit rate do both trips share?
tasks.why: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and 20 ÷ 5 = 4, so both trips go 4 miles per hour.

tasks.q: Why did Marcus say Kira had shown only one case?
options: Two examples do not show that a claim is true for every pair of ratios.
The numbers in her example were too large.
Miles per hour is the wrong unit to use.
tasks.why: A claim about every pair needs a reason that works for every case, not only the examples that were checked.

story.title: The Fair Fee Plan
story.goal: convince the council that a plan is fair, using evidence
story.intro: Zuri wants the student council to approve a plan for club fees. She must make a claim, show evidence, and be ready when someone asks, what if it does not work?

beats.lead: Zuri states her claim in one clear sentence before she shows any numbers.
beats.success: The council knows exactly what she wants to prove, and her table matches the claim.
beats.redirect: The council is confused about the claim, so Zuri restates it and points to the evidence.

beats.lead: A council member challenges the plan with a different example.
beats.success: Zuri tests the example and shows it either supports the claim or breaks it.
beats.redirect: Zuri is not sure whether the example works, so she checks the ratio in two rows.

beats.lead: The council asks Zuri to explain why the plan works for every club, not only for three.
beats.success: Zuri gives a reason that works for every case and the council nods.
beats.redirect: Her reason covers only the clubs she tested, so Zuri looks for a rule that works for all.

story.ending: The council makes a decision, and Zuri can explain which parts of her argument were evidence and which were reasons.

panels.says: My claim is that if 4 pens cost 6 dollars, then 10 pens cost 15 dollars.
What is your evidence?
6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 dollars per pen, and 10 × 1.5 = 15 dollars.
Good evidence, but it only works if every pen costs the same, with no bulk discount.

predict.q: A store takes 5 dollars off any order of 10 pens. Before Tess answers, predict what happens to Rafa's claim.
options: The claim fails, because 10 pens would cost 10 dollars, not 15 dollars
The claim holds, because 10 pens still cost 15 dollars
The claim holds, because 10 is more than 4
predict.why: 15 − 5 = 10, so 10 pens cost 10 dollars. That is a counterexample to Rafa's claim.

modeling.title: Is the bus pass a fair deal?
modeling.scenario: A fictional student group argues about two ways to pay for the bus. Option A charges for each ride, and Option B is a flat monthly pass.
assumptions: Option A charges the same price for every ride.
Option B costs the same amount no matter how many rides you take.
A student rides the same number of times each week.
prompts: Claim: the cost is proportional to the number of rides. Test it for Option A with 10 and 20 rides.
Test the same claim for Option B with 10 and 20 rides. Is there a counterexample?
At how many rides do the two options cost the same?
limits: Real passes may have extra rules, like a limit on rides, which this model ignores.
A student might ride a different number of times each week.

diagnostic.prompt: Claim: the cost of n pencils at 3 dollars each plus a 4 dollar bag is proportional to n. Is the claim true? Give evidence or a counterexample.
